items.title: Melissa Parke, directora ejecutiva de ICAN: “El riesgo de una guerra nuclear nunca ha sido tan alto como ahora”
items.description: La humanidad nunca había estado tan cerca de la autodestrucción. Así lo advierte el reloj del fin del mundo , una iniciativa que el Boletín de Científicos Atómicos actualiza cada año para alertar sobre los peligros que acechan al planeta. Solo faltan 85 segundos para la medianoche, el símbolo de la aniquilación total, debido a la emergencia climática, la irrupción de la inteligencia artificial y las guerras que amenazan a millones de personas. Además, en pleno auge del militarismo, los países más poderosos han acelerado en la carrera armamentista por ampliar y modernizar sus arsenales nucleares, la razón por la que el también llamado reloj del apocalipsis se dio a conocer por primera vez en 1947. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Crece la presión diplomática para socorrer a la población ucrania de Oleshki, azotada por el hambre tras la ocupación rusa
items.description: Algo se mueve en la esfera diplomática en torno a la grave crisis humanitaria que sufre Oleshki, una localidad de la región ucrania de Jersón ocupada por los rusos . “Es duro llamar vida a eso”, deplora Vitalii Mikolaiovich, de 55 años, que consiguió escapar el mes pasado de la población, donde apenas hay comida. El Papa León XIV ha abordado con los presidentes de Rusia, Vladímir Putin, y Ucrania, Volodímir Zelenski , una posible tregua que permita evacuar a los civiles. En torno a 6.000 personas, varias decenas de ellas menores, entre Oleshki y alrededores, sufren una clara falta de alimentos y medicinas unida a las duras condiciones de vida por la invasión militar, que les impiden moverse a lugares donde abastecerse. items.title: A rubber-stamp parliament
items.description: IN a democracy, parliament is not only supposed to legislate; it is also expected to safeguard the national interest and deliberate on key policy matters. That criterion does not seem to apply to our parliament. One seldom witnesses a major foreign or national security issue being deliberated by the ‘representatives’ of the people, and there is hardly any meaningful debate even on critical constitutional amendments and legislation. This ineffectiveness of the country’s highest legislative body reflects the sorry state of democracy against the backdrop of creeping authoritarianism. Last week, both Houses of parliament approved, within hours and by a two-thirds majority, the decision to remove an elected provincial government and impose a state of emergency and governor’s rule , with no substantive debate. A highly controversial matter was disposed of within hours, with some ministers and leaders of the ruling coalition justifying the action against a provincial government that enjoyed the support of a majority of the members of the assembly, and the arrest of its chief minister and members of his government. It was obvious that the decision had already been taken elsewhere, and that a parliament of debatable legitimacy was, as usual, expected to rubber-stamp it. Most members may not even have understood the constitutional provisions invoked to declare a state of emergency in a province, or whether those provisions applied to the conditions at hand. It looked like a puppet show. But it was not the first time this parliament blindly toed the line. Over the past two years, it has passed the 26th and 27th Amendments , virtually destroying the essence of a Constitution that rests on the independence of the judiciary. That was perhaps the most shameful moment in our parliamentary history: ministers were shown the draft only hours before the session, and members were handed it on the floor of the House. Most had not read it when they voted for amendments of critical importance. They were passed overnight. One can hardly recollect a foreign or national security policy being debated in parliament, nor even in its committees; one wonders whether such policies are discussed and approved by the cabinet at all. The main reason the government has given for its action in KP is that the provincial government was unwilling to cooperate in counterterrorism operations in the province worst hit by the resurgence of militant violence. The ruling coalition is bound to pay a heavy political price for its undemocratic actions. But a question that is never answered is whether the state has a well-defined, overarching counterterrorism policy in place, and, if it does, whether that policy has ever been discussed in cabinet, let alone presented before parliament or any of its committees for deliberation. The truth is that we have no clarity on how to deal with this existential threat. Over the past quarter of a century I have covered and written extensively on Pakistan’s struggle with terrorism, and I can vouch that we have never had a holistic approach to an issue for which the state itself has been responsible. Even now, as militant attacks claim the lives of an increasing number of security personnel, the state is pursuing a one-dimensional policy that relies solely on kinetic operations in the affected areas, with little success. The confusion persists despite the claims of the ‘hard state’. Balochistan, another strategically located province, has been bleeding for over 25 years with rising separatist militancy. As a result, the state has now lost control of large parts of the province, with an unrepresentative provincial government at the helm. Yet neither the cabinet nor parliament has any say in such a grave national security matter. While the ousted provincial government is being held responsible for the worsening situation in KP, who is responsible for the state of affairs in Balochistan? The reality is that the policy on Balochistan lies outside the domain of the present civilian set-up or the so-called representative parliament. Unsurprisingly, a critical foreign policy question — Pakistan’s signing of the trilateral Makkah Joint Defence Agreement — has not been ratified, or more precisely rubber-stamped, by parliament. Turkiye, the other signatory to the pact, is still waiting for its parliament to endorse it. It is an extremely important external and internal policy issue, with long-term implications for a country already facing multiple challenges. There is also the question of whether the pact will be activated with the escalation in the Houthis’ attacks on Saudi Arabia. While a pliant parliament has been conveniently used to rubber-stamp controversial constitutional amendments and laws that curb judicial independence and freedom of expression, there has also been much talk about resetting the country’s administrative structure. The all-powerful and ubiquitous interior minister has publicly declared that the system has collapsed and called for a complete revamp. But what does this projected resetting mean for the present hybrid power structure and for parliament? There are strong views that emergency rule in KP could be the first step towards extending it to the entire country. Will a parliament that has endorsed emergency rule in KP also rubber-stamp any such action, even though it would further curtail its own powers? One objective of emergency rule is to clear the ground for the resetting of administrative units, an extremely volatile issue for some of the coalition parties, particularly the PPP. The Sindh Assembly has already voted against administrative changes. Still, with the legitimacy question hanging over its head, it would be extremely hard for parliament to resist a measure that would further consolidate authoritarian rule in the country. The ruling coalition — which has feverishly supported emergency rule in KP, the controversial constitutional amendments that curb judicial independence, and the Peca laws being deployed to control the media — will pay a heavy political price for its undemocratic actions that are paving the way for the winding up of the entire system. The shadow of authoritarianism looms over the country as a parliament with a dubious mandate has already surrendered whatever little power it had left. The collapse of a system built on a mandate seen as stolen seems imminent, with its patrons planning a new setup. It will be a further leap backward, taking an already unstable state down a dangerous path. The writer is an author and journalist. zhussain100@yahoo.com X: @hidhussain Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: ‘It is never your fault’ — advocate tells sexual abuse survivors
items.description: A co-founder of On This Side, Amtu Akumfi-Ameyaw, has urged survivors of sexual abuse to reject self-blame, stressing that responsibility for abuse rests with the perpetrators and not the victims. She said adults had a duty to protect children and ensure their safety and that survivors needed constant reassurance that they were not to blame for what had happened to them. “We have to keep reminding survivors that it is never their fault. It is never your fault,” she said on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, October 20. “If you’re a survivor listening to me today, if you have a child that’s a survivor, if you have happened to become a parent yourself and you were a survivor when you were a lot younger, this is a reminder that it is never your fault.” Her comments come amid national concern over allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), where headmaster Zakaria Abdulai has been interdicted by the Ghana Education Service (GES) and arrested by the police as investigations continue. The case has attracted widespread attention following reports by JoyNews investigative correspondent Manasseh Azure Awuni. Ms Akumfi-Ameyaw said adults entrusted with the care of children must be held to their responsibility to protect them from harm. “Adults are supposed to be responsible. Adults are supposed to protect you and make sure that you are safe. So it is never your fault that they abused you,” she said. Abuse cuts across school levels Ms Akumfi-Ameyaw said cases of sexual abuse were not confined to senior high schools, citing experiences involving children at primary and junior high school levels. She recounted the experience of a colleague who had been abused in a classroom at the age of eight, almost nine, and who was now in tertiary education. She also referred to a separate case involving a 12-year-old girl approaching her 13th birthday, in which her organisation had helped secure a conviction. In that case, she said, the perpetrator was someone close to the child’s family. Ms Akumfi-Ameyaw said her organisation had also received cases involving alleged abuse by teachers, underscoring the need for children to be protected in schools and other settings where adults exercise authority over them. Her examples highlighted the different circumstances in which abuse can occur and the importance of taking disclosures seriously, regardless of a child’s age or relationship to the alleged perpetrator. Calls for stronger action The advocate also criticised what she described as failures to adequately protect students, saying those working to expose abuse had to be prepared to speak out despite resistance. “I know that I keep saying that. I know that abusers are not happy with me this week, but that’s not why we do the work. We do the work because we need to see results,” she said. She added: “And I would repeat that good girls don’t get the jobs done. Only the people that are ready to take the risk and are ready to put their voices out there.”

items.title: Missing lawmakers
items.description: FOLLOWING the imposition of emergency and governor’s rule in KP on Oct 11, many lawmakers of the PTI remain untraceable. The matter has been raised in parliament and in the courts. During a hearing of related petitions in the Peshawar High Court yesterday, PTI chairman Gohar Ali Khan said that 12 MNAs and 14 MPAs belonging to the KP Assembly had been “picked up”. Soon after the proclamation of emergency, Federal Minister of State for Interior Talal Chaudhry had confirmed that KP’s non-functional Chief Minister Sohail Afridi and some members of his cabinet were in “preventive custody”. Meanwhile, on Monday, PTI lawmakers in the National Assembly demanded production orders for their fellow party MNAs. Opposition Leader Mahmood Achakzai endorsed the demand, while Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in the Senate, raised the issue in the Upper House. One PTI MNA has been arrested at his madressah in Bannu, but the whereabouts of most of the missing lawmakers remain unknown, with their families also in the dark. Some lawmakers have reportedly been in detention since before Oct 11. This is not the first time that opposition lawmakers in Pakistan have gone ‘missing’. The proclamation of emergency should not, however, mean holding fundamental rights in abeyance. Whether it is members of the assemblies, or ordinary citizens, the Constitution — if that document still holds any value for the wielders of power — guarantees due process to every Pakistani. Therefore, Mr Afridi, as well as other PTI lawmakers, must be produced before the courts forthwith. The state must announce publicly what they are accused of, so that they can defend themselves, and engage counsel of their choice. Mr Chaudhry had said that if there are cases against the PTI leaders they would be charged, and if no evidence is found against them they would be released. The state must keep its promise, and also grant the lawmakers access to their families. Members of the ruling coalition — belonging to both the PML-N and PPP — were on the receiving end of the state’s excesses during their time in opposition. Perhaps they should remember their own experiences, and the commitments their leaders made to upholding the rule of law. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: El Constitucional se dispone a rechazar el amparo presentado por la ‘ley de nietos’
items.description: Una mayoría de los doce magistrados que componen el Tribunal Constitucional defenderá este miércoles que se inadmita el recurso de amparo presentado por el Defensor del Pueblo, según fuentes del órgano de garantías. El recurso pedía restablecer el derecho al voto de más de 160.000 españoles, nacionalizados en virtud de la ley de nietos , que viven en el extranjero y a quien el Tribunal Supremo ha retirado cautelarmente el sufragio a poco más de un mes de las próximas elecciones generales. La mayoría del Pleno, sin reflejar esta vez la división de referencia entre progresistas y conservadores, considera que como el Supremo abrió un plazo de alegaciones para los afectados —vigente hasta el viernes, 23 de octubre—, el recurso del Defensor es prematuro y no cumple con el requisito de subsidiariedad del amparo: esto es, que se haya agotado la vía de la justicia ordinaria. items.title: De Tom Cruise a Pedro Sánchez: el eterno mito del hombre que no sabe (o no puede) bailar
items.description: Si la escritora Vicki Baum estaba en lo cierto al decir que uno de los atajos hacia la felicidad es el baile, muchos hombres agradecerán saber que no es necesario que esa danza sea especialmente memorable. De ser así, ese trayecto se volvería mucho más complicado. ¿Por qué hay tantos hombres que temen bailar? ¿Y por qué a tantas mujeres a las que un mal baile les genera verdadero rechazo? En Sorry I Don’t Dance: Why Men Refuse to Move ( Perdona, pero yo no bailo: por qué los hombres se niegan a mover el esqueleto ) (Oxford University Press), Maxine Leeds Craig se pregunta precisamente cómo, tras haber estado asociada la masculinidad durante un tiempo con la gracia, la danza y el movimiento, en la actualidad se considera el baile y la masculinidad se han vuelto incompatibles. “La razón por la que tantos hombres evitan bailar tiene que ver con cómo se percibe su sexualidad. Evitar parecer gay es central a la hora de representar la masculinidad normativa. El miedo a parecer homosexuales les limita a la hora de andar y de gesticular. Determina cómo bailan y evita que algunos bailen jamás”, asegura. En muchísimas películas estadounidenses, especialmente adolescentes, hay una escena primordial en la que el protagonista es pillado en su habitación haciendo algo que considera humillante e íntimo: bailar al ritmo de su canción favorita. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Geoffrey Hinton, el padrino de la IA: “No soy catastrofista. Creo que hay un 1% de posibilidades de que nos destruya”

Ya no lo dice. Ahora se dedica a alertar sobre los peligros de continuar la carrera que él mismo empezó. Confiesa que, en parte, se arrepiente del trabajo al que ha dedicado una vida. Su reconversión de padrino de la IA a profeta de la catástrofe marcó un punto de inflexión en la industria. Sucedió en 2023, cuando abandonó su puesto como vicepresidente de Google entre advertencias funestas. Entonces, algunos vieron su reacción exagerada. Tres años después, muchos han seguido sus pasos. María del Monte: “No he escondido nunca a nadie, ni me he escondido de nadie”
items.description: “Dame la dureza de la verdad, pero no me engañes con una mentira”. Así de tajante demuestra María del Monte (Sevilla, 64 años) lo importante que es para ella la transparencia y la sinceridad. Por eso, en el segundo párrafo del libro que acaba de publicar, Si el corazón se equivoca, se le perdona (HarperCollins) , advierte de que su contenido “no va de su vida”, o al menos, de esa vida que ha asomado en la prensa y los programas del corazón más allá de su trayectoria profesional. “Eso no me interesa, la vida tiene más profundidad como para quedarse en esa capa de superficie”, zanja durante una mañana soleada que desafía los malos augurios de lluvia. La primera incursión de la sevillana en el mundo editorial es una generosa inmersión en sus inquietudes, sus motivaciones, sus zozobras y sus anhelos, que destapa describiendo de una manera franca y natural cómo se ha ido guiando en los ámbitos que para ella son más importantes: su familia, amigos, parejas, seres queridos y ausentes, sus orígenes y tradiciones, y ella misma. “Lo más bonito que me han dicho del libro, y que era mi único objetivo, es que leerlo era como charlar conmigo”, explica sonriente. Seguir leyendo

items.title: El Gobierno de Ayuso se niega a negociar con los profesores en huelga: “Es intolerable, nos están despreciando”
items.description: Una semana después de que comenzara la huelga educativa en Madrid, los planes de la Consejería de Educación no pasan por reunirse con los docentes. No importa que miles de profesores y profesoras de la educación pública no universitaria hayan secundado la movilización con elevados porcentajes de seguimiento según los sindicatos, ni que se hayan manifestado diariamente para insistir en que al otro lado del tablero —el que encabeza la consejera de Educación, Ciencia y Universidades, Mercedes Zarzalejo— se dé un paso hacia el diálogo. Zarzalejo no quiere oír hablar de la huelga, ni de los huelguistas , menos aún de sentarse frente a frente con el Comité de Huelga, al que no reconoce como interlocutor legítimo. “Las reivindicaciones de esta huelga son reivindicaciones que no están al alcance de la gestión educativa de la Comunidad de Madrid”, aseguró la consejera en unas declaraciones el lunes, sus últimas palabras sobre las protestas y a las que remiten desde la Comunidad cuando se les pregunta por la postura del Gobierno madrileño y si tienen previsto sentarse a negociar. items.title: El profesor en prisión por agredir a una decena de alumnos fue sorprendido con un menor en su casa hace dos años
items.description: En junio del 2024, un joven se preocupó porque su hermano menor de edad estaba tardando demasiado en regresar a casa. Como el adolescente tenía un sistema de geolocalización en su móvil que permitía a su familia saber dónde estaba, el hermano mayor lo revisó y comprobó que estaba en un barrio a las afueras de Madrid. Extrañado y preocupado, el chico acudió a esa dirección y se encontró a su hermano, que tenía en aquel momento menos de 16 años, con un profesor de su colegio, las Mercedarias de Don Juan Alarcón, ubicado en el centro de Madrid. La familia puso una denuncia, el docente fue detenido, se ordenó su alejamiento del chico y el colegio lo despidió. Pero esa solo era la punta del iceberg de lo que la policía no duda en definir como un “depredador” sexual de menores. Dos años después de aquello, desde el pasado viernes, ese hombre está en prisión, acusado de haber agredido al menos a una decena de estudiantes más . Seguir leyendo

items.title: Al menos 11 militares han resultado heridos en enfrentamientos con inmigrantes en Ceuta
items.description: Los militares desplegados en Ceuta están en el ojo del huracán. El Hospital Universitario de la ciudad autónoma ha remitido al juzgado de guardia una veintena de partes de lesiones de inmigrantes que dicen haber sido golpeados por miembros de las Fuerzas Armadas. Pero los indocumentados no son los únicos que resultan heridos en estos enfrentamientos que se vienen repitiendo tras la irrupción de más de 70.000 inmigrantes a través del paso del Tarajal los pasados 30 y 31 de julio. Al menos 11 soldados han resultado heridos de diversa consideración desde que el Ejército se desplegó en misión de disuasión, vigilancia y apoyo a las Fuerzas y Cuerpos de Seguridad del Estado, según fuentes de Defensa. El último, el pasado fin de semana, cuando uno de ellos se fracturó un dedo. Varios han sido trasladados al hospital Gómez Ulla de Madrid para someterse a intervenciones quirúrgicas. La mayoría de las lesiones, según las mismas fuentes, se ha producido en el curso de forcejeos y persecuciones, pero también ha habido apedreamientos. El más grave, a finales de agosto en la zona de Benzú, cuando decenas de inmigrantes lanzaron piedras a una patrulla , con un saldo de cuatro soldados heridos y una docena de marroquíes detenidos. Seguir leyendo

items.title: La emisión de tarjetas de transporte se desploma tras endurecer Madrid los requisitos y condicionarlas al empadronamiento
items.description: La emisión de tarjetas de transporte del Consorcio Regional de Madrid (CRTM) se derrumbó un 23,5% en 2026 con respecto a la media de los veranos de 2023, 2024 y 2025 tras endurecerse el criterio de residencia para su obtención. Así lo reflejan los datos obtenidos por EL PAÍS en aplicación de la ley de transparencia, ceñidos al periodo 15 de junio-1 de septiembre para cada año. Aunque la Administración autonómica niega a ese balance capacidad para “establecer una relación causal” entre el descenso y la decisión de condicionar la obtención del título de transporte a la acreditación de la residencia en la región, el cambio, en vigor desde el 15 de junio, ha generado críticas de la oposición por su impacto potencial sobre estudiantes y trabajadores de otras regiones y migrantes no empadronados. La Administración, según un portavoz, calcula que los usuarios no residentes son unos 200.000 (3,4% del total). Seguir leyendo

items.title: USTED professor calls for Ghana-backed research into locally suited drainage solutions
items.description: A coastal engineering and climate adaptation specialist at the University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development (USTED), Professor Isaac Boateng, has urged Ghanaian research funders to invest in studies that identify sustainable drainage solutions suited to local conditions. Speaking at a workshop on teaching Sustainable Drainage Systems (SuDS) in Ghanaian TVET and higher education institutions, Prof. Boateng said research is needed to determine which interventions work best across the country. “I therefore appeal to the Ghana Research Fund to consider investing in sustainable drainage system research in Ghana,” he said. He also appealed to the British Council to consider additional funding for the project. “Given the challenges, the British Council may consider giving the team additional funding to enable us to deal with the additional identified issues,” he said. Prof. Boateng said international experience, including lessons from the United Kingdom, could inform Ghana’s efforts, but warned against adopting designs without adapting them to local conditions. “Successful knowledge transfer does not mean copying designs without considering local realities,” he said, citing Ghana’s rainfall patterns, soil conditions, available materials, land constraints, maintenance capacity and financial circumstances. He said locally generated evidence would help guide engineering practice and public policy, and called for field monitoring, student research and collaboration across disciplines. The workshop addressed flooding and stormwater management challenges in Ghanaian communities. Prof. Boateng cited rapid urbanisation, changing rainfall patterns, expanding impermeable surfaces, blocked drains and encroachment on waterways as factors that can worsen flooding. “Rather than treating stormwater as waste, we must manage it as a resource,” he said. Sustainable drainage approaches can slow runoff, support infiltration and storage, and improve water quality. Examples include rain gardens, permeable pavements, vegetated swales, green roofs and rainwater harvesting. He said these approaches should complement conventional drainage and be selected according to local site conditions. He also called for SuDS concepts to be integrated into existing engineering, construction, environmental management and urban planning courses, with practical learning opportunities for students. “A drainage system is not successful simply because it has been constructed. It must continue to function effectively throughout its service life,” he said, stressing the importance of inspection, maintenance, performance monitoring and long-term cost management. “The drains we design today will influence the safety of our communities tomorrow,” he said. “The skills we teach today will shape the infrastructure of the next generation,” he added. Associate Professor of Real Estate at Edinburgh Napier University and project lead, Dr Cletus Moobela, said the project aims to adapt international knowledge and solutions to Ghanaian conditions. “Our aim is to take solutions developed and applied globally and adapt them to the Ghanaian context,” he said. “We recognise that not every solution will be suitable for Ghana,” he stated. Dr Moobela said the project focuses on education and curriculum development rather than installing drainage systems at individual sites. The team is working with instructors and educational institutions to introduce SuDS into teaching. “Our focus is on the institutions responsible for educating and training future professionals,” he said. The project will assess whether instructors incorporate SuDS into their curricula, gather feedback from students and examine the extent to which educational institutions adopt the approaches. Dr Moobela said graduates entering the built environment would be expected to apply what they learn in their professional careers. Higher Education Project Manager at the British Council in Ghana, Afia Yeboah Agyeman, thanked Edinburgh Napier University and USTED for working together on the project. “I want to say thank you to Edinburgh Napier and USTED for coming together on such an important project,” she said. Afia said drainage problems were a major concern in Ghana and expressed hope that the project would make a positive difference. “We are hoping to see the positive impact that this project will create,” she said. She also hoped the initiative would attract more partnerships and funding so it could expand across other higher education institutions, with SuDS embedded in curricula and educators receiving further training. “Moving forward, [we hope to] draw more partnerships, more funds to support this project on a larger scale across other higher education institutions and embed SuDS in the curriculum, [with] capacity building of teachers,” she said. Afia said the project forms part of the British Council’s work to facilitate transnational education partnerships between Ghanaian institutions and UK universities. The Council facilitated five such partnerships last year, she said, enabling institutions to share expertise and explore ways to work together. The Council is also developing a policy to guide transnational education collaboration.

items.title: Hegseth discusses Iran with Netanyahu in unannounced visit
items.description: JERUSALEM: US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth arrived in Israel on an unannounced visit, and discussed the Iran war with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as tensions continue to simmer between the US and Iran. Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli PM, confirmed that Netanyahu had met Hegseth at the Uvda air force base in Israel’s southern Negev desert region. Mr Netanyahu and Mr Hegseth discussed “the threats in the region” and the US-Israel partnership in dealing both “offensively and defensively” with those threats, he said in a brief phone call. The defence secretary thanked Israel for hosting US forces, which Spielman said numbered in the thousands, and discussed President Donald Trump’s support for the prime minister. Israeli PM celebrates Trump’s endorsement ahead of next week’s election “There’s a deep personal relationship here that was at the core of this discussion,” Spielman said. The Pentagon has not publicly commented on Mr Hegseth’s visit. Earlier, he posted that he had visited US service members in the Central Command area of responsibility, which covers the Middle East, northeast Africa and parts of Asia, but did not specify where he had met the personnel. Hegseth’s visit comes as tensions flare between the US and Iran over the Strait of Hormuz, and Yemen’s Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi Arabia. The Israeli prime minister also said he spoke with President Trump on Sunday about the importance of eliminating the Iranian government. “We are committed to completing the elimination of the Iranian regime,” Mr Netanyahu said in a statement released by his office. “I have discussed this with Trump many times, including the day before yesterday.” Netanyahu basks in Trump endorsement Netanyahu basked in Trump’s endorsement on Monday ahead of close-fought elections, airing a phone call in which the US president predicted he would win, and suggested they may again attack Iran together. “I think you’re going to have a tremendous victory, actually,” the US president can be heard saying on speakerphone. “You’re the man I want by my side, Bibi,” Donald Trump said, referring to Mr Netanyahu by his nickname. Netanyahu, while reminding the famously loose-lipped president that they were on an open line, hailed Trump for joining Israel in attacking Iran in February. “Donald, we have a job to finish,” Netanyahu beamed. “We’ll finish it together. We’ll finish it, and no one else will do it.” Netanyahu did not elaborate, but again described Iran as “the greatest danger”. Trump, 80, and Netanyahu, who turns 77 on Wednesday, have forged a close partnership at a time when both are vastly unpopular in public opinion in most democratic nations. The pair have also managed to avoid prosecution while in power, with Mr Netanyahu facing charges of corruption that could land him in prison. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Subsidy Furore: Experts, opposition take on Oyedele over N4,000/$ crash claim
items.description: * You’re paying fuel subsidy through back door, APM tells Tinubu * NDC kicks, asks why are our refineries not working? * Magnitude cannot be established by assertion alone – Prof Iledare * Minister must show assumptions, economic model underpinning projection — Egbomeade * You’re the Egypt Nigerians’ll never return to, Atiku tackles Tinubu By Henry Umoru, Peter Egwuatu, Udeme Akpan & Luminous Jannamike LAGOS — Some opposition parties and experts yesterday challenged the Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, to explain the assumptions he based his assertion that the Naira might crash to N4,000/$ should the Federal Government restore fuel subsidy. The minister had in an interview on the sidelines of the just-concluded World Bank/IMF meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, said the local currency would crash to N4,000/$, if subsidy was restored. Some opposition presidential candidates, including African Democratic Congress’ Atiku Abubakar; Social Democratic Party’s Adewole Adebayo; and Nigeria Democratic Party’s Peter Obi, had in the past few weeks, said they would restore fuel subsidy, if they were elected president to assuage the sufferings of the people. Aside from Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, and Allied People’s Movement, APM, which disagreed with the finance minister’s assertion, experts, including petroleum experts, Prof. Wumi Iledare; and Economic and Communications expert, Clifford Egbomeade, also challenged him to explain the assumptions on which he based his assertions. Reacting to the minister’s declaration, the APM accused President Bola Tinubu’s administration of paying fuel subsidy through the back door, questioning the recent petrol price reduction, despite government’s declaration that subsidy was gone. The party also dismissed Oyedele’s warning that restoring subsidy could push the naira to N4,000 per dollar, describing the projection as unfounded and accusing the government of pursuing economic policies driving businesses into closure. APM National Secretary, Ayodele Adebayo, who stated this in a response to Vanguard’s inquiries, faulted the administration’s handling of fuel prices and its claims about investors’ loss of confidence in opposition parties. “What are they doing now with the current reduction in petrol price for one month? Is it not returning subsidy through the back door?” Adebayo queried. He argued that the naira had previously exchanged at a stronger rate, rejecting the minister’s projection as an attempt to justify the government’s position on subsidy. Adebayo also challenged Oyedele’s claims that investors had written off opposition parties as unserious, alleging that harsh economic policies had forced several companies to shut down. “Where are even the investors the Minister of Finance, Taiwo Oyedele, is talking about? Is it the recycled ones by the present administration?” he queried. The APM secretary said his party favoured an appropriate pricing framework for petroleum products to prevent further hardship, insisting that Nigerians should not be left with little money after paying for fuel. “We cannot subscribe to seeing Nigerians use all their entitlements and earnings to buy fuel due to harsh economic policies,” Adebayo said. NDC kicks, asks why are our refineries not working? Similarly, the national leadership of the NDC slammed Oyedele for his statement, describing it as a subtle blackmail. National Publicity Secretary of the NDC, Osa Director accused the All Progressives Congress, APC-led government of mortgaging a sizeable portion of Nigeria’s crude oil to take foreign loans “to the extent that we are unable to supply Dangote refinery the needed crude oil to satisfy domestic consumption and demand.” Osa Director said: “The most important aspect of the subsidy conversation is not yet addressed. Why are our refineries not working? Why did the APC government mortgage a sizeable portion of our crude oil to take foreign loans, to the extent that we are unable to supply Dangote refinery the needed crude oil to satisfy domestic consumption and demand? “If all these and the criminality in the subsidy regime are addressed, the doomsday prediction of the Minister of Finance would not be necessary.” The ADC had taken a similar position in its reaction to the issue on Monday. Magnitude cannot be established by assertion alone — Prof Iledare Examing the minister’s statement in an interview with Vanguard yesterday, Petroleum Economist, Prof. Wumi Iledare, said: “The petrol subsidy debate should be guided by fiscal sustainability, market efficiency and measurable public welfare, not political rhetoric or unsupported forecasts. “Restoring the subsidy would require the government to finance the gap between the regulated price and petrol’s economic cost. Depending on its scale and design, this could increase fiscal pressure, borrowing, foreign-exchange demand, import dependence, smuggling and arbitrage. “However, the claim that subsidy restoration would push the naira to N4,000 per US dollar should be treated as a risk scenario, not an inevitable outcome. ‘’Finance Minister, Taiwo Oyedele, has linked such a possibility to capital flight and weaker investor confidence if reforms are reversed. These are plausible channels, but the specific exchange-rate projection requires evidence and clearly-stated assumptions. “The naira is influenced by foreign-exchange supply and demand, crude-oil receipts, domestic production, capital flows, reserves, monetary policy and investor confidence. Subsidy restoration could add depreciation pressure, but its magnitude cannot be established by assertion alone. “Subsidy removal, however, should not be judged only by its fiscal benefits. Higher petrol prices affect transport, food distribution, production costs and household welfare. Savings matter only when converted into productive investment, infrastructure, efficient public transport and targeted support for vulnerable households. “Nigeria should, therefore, assess both options against affordability, fiscal sustainability, energy security and public value. Any restoration proposal should disclose its cost per litre, total fiscal exposure, funding source, beneficiaries, anti-leakage safeguards and exit strategy. ‘’If removal continues, the government must show how the savings are being used and what measurable welfare gains citizens receive. “Nigeria needs neither cheap petrol at any cost nor expensive petrol in the name of reform. It needs competitive petroleum markets, efficient energy supply, transparent governance and targeted support.” Minister must show assumptions, economic model underpinning projection — Egbomeade Reacting in a similar manner, Clifford Egbomeade , Economics and Communications expert, said: “Rather than restore blanket fuel subsidies, the government should address the structural factors driving petrol prices, particularly exchange-rate volatility, domestic refining capacity and distribution costs. ‘’The government must also disclose how much subsidy removal has saved and how those savings have been spent, and the measurable economic benefits achieved. “The minister’s N4,000/$ projection describes a possible risk, not an inevitable outcome. Subsidy restoration could widen the fiscal deficit, undermine investor confidence and increase foreign-exchange demand, particularly if fuel imports rise. ‘’However, the minister must show the assumptions and economic model underpinning the projection. The naira’s value also depends on oil revenues, foreign-exchange supply, capital flows and monetary policy. ‘’Policy-makers must evaluate subsidy restoration against its fiscal cost, impact on household purchasing power and implications for exchange-rate stability, rather than rely on political promises or forecasts not supported by evidence.” This may not be an exaggeration – Adonri However, David Adonri, an economist and Managing Director, HighCap Securities Limited, said: “The removal of subsidy on petrol has achieved several objectives for government. First, it ended the issuance of public debt to finance the consumption subsidy. It repaired the damaged balance sheet of NNPC which could not remit revenue to government while the subsidy lasted. As a result of savings from subsidy removal, the federation account has more distributable income which has restored the financial health of sub-nationals. For the public sector in general, the policy has produced unimaginable financial turnaround and revived the integrity of the Petroleum industry. It has enabled domestic production to become competitive and viable. ‘’That without removal of fuel subsidy, the value of the Naira now would have crashed to N4,000/$ as expressed by the Minister of Finance. This may not be an exaggeration. While the public sector has enjoyed all the benefits accruing from subsidy, unfortunately, it has left in its trail the worst cost of living crisis ever experienced by consumers in the country. ‘’This is because of the inability of the fiscal authorities to run an effective supply side policy to enhance agriculture and mining due to rural insecurity, close the expanding housing deficit and drive the use of alternative sources of energy such as solar and CNG. You’re the Egypt Nigerians’ll never return to, Atiku tackles Tinubu On President Bola Tinubu’s declaration that Nigeria would not return to Egypt, following calls by the opposition for fuel subsidy to be restored, presidential candidate of African Democratic Congress, ADC, Atiku Abubakar, said the statement exposed “how little he (President) understands the suffering of Nigerians”. In a statement issued on his behalf by Phrank Shaibu, Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Atiku said Tinubu boasted of removing the subsidy on his first day in office “like a wicked king recounting the suffering he had inflicted as a triumph.” He said: “Bola, you are the Egypt Nigerians are desperate to escape. You celebrate the day you made fuel more expensive, then lecture families struggling to pay for food and transport about why they must never go back.” “At least, Pharaoh knew he was holding people captive. Tinubu watches families cut meals, workers spend their salaries on transport and businesses struggle to keep their lights on, then tells them a story about Moses. ‘’He may quote scripture, but he governs like Pharaoh, Herod and Ahab combined: deaf to the cries of the people, proud of the hardship he has imposed and convinced that power excuses him from answering for it. “Bola, a mother trying to feed her children cannot pay for food with a metaphor. A worker cannot get to work on a story about the Red Sea. Nigerians are asking how you intend to make life affordable. Answer them. “I will make life affordable again through practical relief Nigerians can feel. My proposal is clear: give limited, budgeted support only to verified petroleum products refined in Nigeria and sold to Nigerians. ‘’Imported fuel gets nothing. Independent auditors must track every naira, and the benefit must reach consumers in the price they pay. If it does not lower that price, it has failed its purpose. “But hardship is not the only captivity Nigerians face. Tinubu’s failure on security cannot be buried under Buhari’s record. He asked Nigerians for the presidency knowing that communities were under attack, families were paying ransom and children were afraid to travel to school. ‘’He took the oath to protect them. Yet his own campaign Director-General asks, ‘What do you expect Tinubu to do when even Buhari, a general, could not wipe out insecurity?’ Let me remind them that President Yar’Adua was not a sergeant, yet he stamped it out. “Nigerians expect their President to confront the killers, rescue the abducted and make it possible to travel, farm, work and sleep without fear. If Tinubu cannot tell them how he will do that after more than three years in office, he has no business asking for four more years. ‘’The lives lost under his watch are not an argument about his predecessor. They are an indictment of his own leadership. And look at what Tinubu asks of the officers sent to protect us. ‘’A retired Assistant Superintendent told me he receives ₦29,000 a month. Serving officers are drawing down their pension savings to feed their families. How can a President demand courage from police officers in the field while leaving them worried about food at home and destitution in retirement? “Bola, answer the retired officers asking for a pension they can live on. Act on the Police Exit Bill and review serving officers’ salaries, as was done for members of the Armed Forces. Give the people who protect Nigerians the pay, healthcare and retirement security their service has earned. “Stop pointing to Egypt as though it lies behind us. For millions of Nigerians, Egypt is the hunger, fear and indignity they are living through under you. They deserve affordable fuel, safe communities and police officers who can serve without sacrificing their families’ future. Tinubu made life expensive. I will make life affordable again.” Vanguard News The post Subsidy Furore: Experts, opposition take on Oyedele over N4,000/$ crash claim appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: ‘Some schoolgirls position themselves to sexually exploit teachers for their money’ – Teacher alleges
items.description: A teacher at Ekumpoano Catholic Basic School, Stephen Desu, has raised concerns about alleged transactional sexual relationships between teachers and female students, saying some girls seek money from teachers in exchange for sex while others may be drawn into such arrangements because of financial hardship. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, October 20, during a discussion on allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), Mr Desu said the issue had different dimensions and required attention to the financial pressures facing students. “There are girls in schools who position themselves to sexually exploit teachers for their money whilst teachers get sex from them in a transactional relationship,” he said. He cited concerns about students’ access to food and money, saying some teachers had allegedly given female students money during periods when food provision in schools was a concern, with sex exchanged in return. “Especially when this food issue came up in our schools, where they’re not getting food. Some teachers stepped up, and they were giving the girls money, and they were exchanging sex for the money they were giving them,” he said. Mr Desu urged parents to consider how their daughters were meeting their needs when they were away at school, particularly when they received little financial support from home. “If you leave your girl child in school and you don’t support her with money and she’s surviving, you as a parent, what makes you think that that child is surviving just because she’s just there?” he asked. Calls for vigilance and accountability The teacher said the profession had a responsibility to protect students while acknowledging that misconduct could occur among a large workforce. “I mean, all professions can boast, but the teacher taught them all. So we position ourselves as the noble profession. Unfortunately, if you have more than 300,000 persons in your classroom as teachers, you may get such persons as predators,” he said. His comments came amid heightened public scrutiny of alleged sexual abuse involving more than 14 female students at Obuasi SHTS. The school’s headmaster, Zakaria Abdulai, has been interdicted by the Ghana Education Service (GES) and arrested by the police as investigations continue. The case has attracted widespread attention following reports by JoyNews investigative correspondent Manasseh Azure Awuni. The case has prompted renewed debate about student protection, the handling of complaints of sexual misconduct and the responsibilities of school authorities. While Mr Desu described some relationships as transactional, any sexual relationship between a teacher and a student raises serious concerns about the imbalance of power and the teacher’s duty of care. Financial vulnerability can also make students more susceptible to coercion or exploitation.

items.title: IA: l’ONU met en garde contre l’essor des systèmes d’armes autonomes
items.description: L’Institut des Nations Unies pour la recherche sur le désarmement (UNIDIR) a mis en garde contre les risques croissants liés à l’utilisation de l’intelligence artificielle dans le domaine militaire, appelant à renforcer la coopération internationale et les mécanismes de régulation afin de préserver la paix et la sécurité internationales. « La guerre menée par des machines se rapproche à grands pas », a déclaré le directeur de l’UNIDIR, Robin Geiss, lors d’un point de presse tenu lundi au siège new-yorkais de l’ONU, soulignant que l’enjeu est de savoir si les machines seront autorisées à sélectionner et à tuer des êtres humains. L’IA et les systèmes autonomes sont déjà utilisés dans l’analyse du renseignement, l’identification des cibles, les drones, les cyberattaques et les opérations d’influence, a-t-il relevé, avertissant que l’accélération des cycles de décision réduit la marge de jugement humain et accroît les risques d’erreur, de mauvaise interprétation et d’escalade, y compris dans le domaine nucléaire. Face à ces défis, l’UNIDIR a lancé à Genève un Centre d’excellence sur l’IA, la paix et la sécurité, a fait savoir le responsable onusien. Plusieurs initiatives seront présentées également à New York, notamment un forum multipartite, un cadre volontaire de conduite responsable destiné aux entreprises technologiques, ainsi qu’un lexique visant à harmoniser les notions liées à la sécurité et à l’autonomie militaires, a dit M. Geiss. Une autre initiative portera sur les risques de détournement de l’IA par des groupes armés non étatiques, des réseaux criminels et des organisations terroristes. L’UNIDIR entend également soutenir les travaux préparatoires au Sommet de l’IA de Genève, prévu en juin 2027. Les déclarations de M. Geiss interviennent à la veille de la Semaine de désarmement (24-30 octobre), qui vise, depuis 1995, à promouvoir la sensibilisation et une meilleure compréhension par le public des questions de désarmement et de leur importance transversale. The post IA: l’ONU met en garde contre l’essor des systèmes d’armes autonomes appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: Pakistan warns India against attempt to alter strategic balance
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Adviser to the National Command Authority retired Lt Gen Khalid Kidwai on Tuesday warned that Pakistan could review its deployment options to restore strategic balance in South Asia, saying India was moving towards a more prepared, potentially first-use capable nuclear posture. “Pakistan never has and never will accept strategic imbalances to be induced in South Asia,” Mr Kidwai said at the second Islamabad Non-Proliferation Conference, hosted by the Strategic Vision Institute, an Islamabad based think tank specialising in strategic issues. “Pakistan will review and reconsider all options for appropriate deployments in order to restore the strategic balance and strategic stability while retaining the policy of strategic ambiguity,” he added. Mr Kidwai and retired Lt Gen Sarfraz Sattar, both former heads of the Strategic Plans Division and advisers to the NCA, said India’s reported deployment of nuclear weapons aboard a submarine, alongside missile modernisation and recent military confrontations, raised the risk of escalation between the two neighbouring arch rivals. NCA adviser reminds India of Pakistan’s Full Spectrum Deterrence policy Nuclear warheads Citing the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute’s SIPRI Yearbook 2026 and other publicly available information, they pointed to reports that India had deployed around 12 nuclear warheads on a submarine for deterrence patrols. They also cited missile canisterisation and wider nuclear and conventional modernisation as developments that cast doubt on India’s declared No-First-Use policy. Mr Kidwai said the reported deployment suggested India had mated nuclear warheads with submarine launched ballistic missiles and begun sea based deterrence patrols. “I do not see any reason as to why an SIPRI report might be inaccurate or speculative,” he said. “This irresponsible escalatory transition towards creating asymmetry in nuclear posture will have profound destabilising effects on South Asian strategic stability,” he added. Mr Kidwai said India’s ability to maintain a continuous at sea deterrent further undermined the credibility of its No-First-Use policy and pointed to a more offensive nuclear posture. “The operational reality that emerges is that India can undertake a first strike against Pakistan at zero notice,” he said. Advance notification He also questioned the absence of advance notification for Indian submarine launched ballistic missile tests, warning that such developments could heighten the risk of miscalculation during a crisis. Referring to the February 2019 confrontation, he said India had reportedly deployed its Arihant nuclear submarine in the Indian Ocean after carrying out air strikes near Balakot in Pakistan, presumably with nuclear weapons aboard. He described the latest reported deployment as part of India’s wider effort to operationalise mated nuclear weapons on submarines. “Pakistan reserves the right to undertake all appropriate measures to safeguard its national security and preserve strategic balance in the region under all circumstances,” Mr Kidwai said. He urged India to understand the implications of Pakistan’s Full Spectrum Deterrence policy. “India in fact will be well advised to read and re-read Pakistan’s policy of Full Spectrum Deterrence and seriously absorb its wide ranging implications for strategic deterrence, strategic stability, and for India’s security,” he said. Mr Sattar said the May 2025 conflict between the nuclear-armed neighbours showed how quickly conventional hostilities could escalate. The ceasefire came after both sides used cruise and ballistic missiles and India deployed strategic naval assets, he said. He drew parallels with the 2019 confrontation, when Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi referred to the deployment of nuclear submarines for deterrence patrols and the positioning of BrahMos missiles along Pakistan’s border. The May 2025 fighting was more intense, involving kamikaze drones, supersonic BrahMos missiles capable of carrying conventional or nuclear warheads, and cyber and electronic warfare, he said. “It is now clear that the 2025 conflict was much more lethal in comparison to the 2019 conflict,” Mr Sattar said, warning that the fighting risked spiralling towards nuclear escalation through accident or miscalculation. He cited India’s canisterisation of land and sea based missiles, pursuit of multiple independently targetable reentry vehicle (MIRV) capabilities, short-range tactical missiles, ballistic missile defences, hypersonic weapons and autonomous platforms as further sources of concern. Combined with India’s Cold Start doctrine, wider military modernisation and the absence of a bilateral arms control mechanism, these developments raised doubts about its No-First-Use declaration and traditionally recessed deterrence posture, he said. “Rather, as I said, it signals a shift towards more first use capable posture,” Mr Sattar said. “The future strategic stability in South Asia is placed on a perilous and worrisome course with heightened risk of misunderstanding and miscalculation, potentially leading to unintended or accidental escalation to the nuclear level,” he added. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Obuasi SHTS: ‘You are supposed to be the protector’ — Safeguarding Lead questions school’s response
items.description: Ashesi University’s Safeguarding Lead, Dr Millicent Adjei, has questioned Obuasi Senior High Technical School’s response to safeguarding concerns. She says children entrusted to a school must feel safe enough to report abuse. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, she identified two failures in the accounts presented. These were boundary crossings between staff and students, and an environment that discouraged children from speaking up. “When you are given that duty of care, you are supposed to be the protector. You are supposed to create that environment where children will be able to come to you, right?” Dr Adjei is Ashesi University’s Director of International Programs and Campus Cohesion, and its Safeguarding Lead. Her comments follow Manasseh Azure Awuni’s investigation, Inside the Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow . It examines allegations of sexual abuse against Obuasi SHTS headmaster Zakaria Abdulai. The investigation found that authorities received complaints months before they suspended him. The Ghana Education Service has interdicted the headmaster pending investigations. A complaint has also been lodged with the police. Dr Adjei said the first boundary was crossed when children were allowed to run personal errands for staff. “Where children are going to the headmaster’s house, that is the first level that shouldn’t have happened,” she said. She argued that asking students to collect and carry food was inappropriate in itself. Her concern extended beyond where the food was delivered. The second failure, she said, concerned students’ confidence in the school’s reporting system. Referring to an account discussed on the programme, she said a girl had not felt comfortable reporting her experiences herself. “It took the girl’s house prefect to go and report, and the girl had several experiences.” Dr Adjei also cited an account of the girl being hospitalised after being caned. She said nothing had been done about it. For her, these accounts raised questions about whether the school had created conditions in which children could seek help. “So the second layer, where an environment that doesn’t support speaking up when some of these things happen, was also broken,” she said. She maintained that the school’s responsibility included giving students the confidence to approach someone with their concerns. “The school did not create that environment for the children, for the young children to be able to have that confidence to report to anyone.”

items.title: BYD to rely on imports initially, Hubco says
items.description: KARACHI: Hub Power Company (Hubco) has said that BYD vehicle production will initially rely entirely on imported raw materials and components, with localisation increasing gradually over time. The long-term objective is to localise up to 80 per cent of the vehicle, which should improve cost competitiveness and reduce reliance on imports, Hubco management said during a corporate briefing held on October 20, 2026. Topline Securities said the BYD plant is expected to commence operations within the next 4-5 weeks, by mid-December. The management is targeting an initial sales run rate of approximately 1,000-1,500 BYD vehicles per month as production ramps up. BYD plans to introduce additional models through a phased approach, focusing on segments that can generate meaningful sales volumes, the brokerage house said. According to Topline Securities, Lucky Cement told analysts on Tuesday that competition in the EV segment remains intense, particularly from Chinese completely built-up (CBU) vehicles. The company aims to begin local production of EV models by the first quarter of calendar year 2027, with volumes and model offerings expected to increase gradually in subsequent quarters. items.title: Text of the Makkah defence agreement
items.description: FOLLOWING its submission for parliamentary approval, Turkish state broadcaster TRT Haber and other outlets have published the text of the Makkah Joint Defence agreement. The 16 articles of the trilateral defence agreement are reproduced here. The Government of the Republic of Turkiye, the Government of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, and the Government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia (hereinafter referred to as a “party”, the “parties”, or the “core parties”). Article 1 : The “parties” shall cooperate to ensure and safeguard one another’s independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and the inviolability of their internationally recognised borders. If the territorial integrity, sovereignty, or internationally recognised borders of any of the “parties” are threatened or endangered, the “parties” shall use all necessary means to eliminate such threat(s) or danger(s). Article 2 : An externally originating armed attack against any of the “parties” shall be considered an attack against all the “parties.” If one of the “parties” is subjected to an armed attack or military aggression by another country or group of countries, the “parties” shall immediately assist the attacked “party,” making full use of all means of mutual assistance that they can provide to one another. For this purpose, to enable the exercise of the right of self-defence recognised by Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations, the “parties” shall determine the scope and nature of the support to be provided following an objective assessment of the assistance required, and shall cooperate within the limits of their available resources, including military means and capabilities. Article 3 : Pursuant to Article 2 of this agreement, the “parties” shall cooperate closely in the fields of defence, defence industry, and security; develop relations among their Armed Forces; and carry out agreed activities aimed at strengthening cooperation in defence. Article 4 : The “parties” shall hold regular consultations on international security matters. They shall continuously and effectively assist one another and cooperate in developing individual and joint measures based on common assessments, in or­­d­­er to protect their vital interests and national security and eliminate thre­ats and dangers to their national security. Article 5 : The “parties” shall stren­­gthen existing cooperation and joint efforts, including at the operational level, in combating terrorism in all its forms and manifestations that adversely affect regional and international stability and security. Article 6 : In wartime and peacetime, the “parties” shall encourage reciprocal personnel exchanges am­­ong defence institutions, joint training programmes and exercises, and deployments and activities aimed at increasing the interoperability of the “parties’” armed forces, in order to develop their defence capabilities. Article 7 : To strengthen their defence capabilities, the “parties” shall, on the basis of mutual agreement, support technology sharing among defence-industry institutions, joint technology development, joint production, and cooperation among defence-industry organisations in the following areas: a) Encouraging joint production in the field of defence; b) Implementing defence innovation through joint research and development projects in technologies requiring specialised expertise; c) Training personnel and supporting the military industry within the territories of the “parties” through experts from any “party”; d) Sharing expertise and lessons learned in the fields of defence industry, defence research and development, and innovation; e) Other areas of cooperation mutually agreed upon by the “parties”. Article 8: The “core parties” shall establish a “Strategic Political and Defe­nce Committee”, comprising the For­e­­ign Ministers, Defence Ministers, and Chiefs of General Staff of the “parties” to provide strategic direction for joint defence, develop defe­nce and security cooperation among the “parties” and address obstacles that may arise during the implementation of this agreement. The Comm­ittee shall meet twice a year, with hosting rotating among the “parties”. The leaders of the “parties” may meet once a year if deemed necessary. The “Strategic Political and Defe­­­nce Committee” may establish subcommittees if it considers this necessary. Agreements or protocols shall, where necessary, be negotiated among the “parties” for the implementation of the areas of cooperation envisaged in this agreement. The “Strategic Political and Def­ence Committee” shall be authorised, by consensus of the “core parties”, to determine and approve the procedures and principles governing the accession of other “parties” to this agreement. A Secretariat headquartered in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia shall be established to serve the “Strategic Political and Defence Committee”. The Secre­tariat shall conclude a headquarters agreement with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The procedures and principles governing the Secretariat’s functioning, organisational structure, and establishment shall subsequently be determined by consensus of the “core parties”. The Secretariat shall be headed by a Secretary-General appointed for a three-year term on a rotational basis among the “core parties”. The first Secretary-General shall be a citizen of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan. The provisions of this Article shall not prejudice the work of existing military cooperation committees among the “parties”. Article 9: To deepen cooperation in intelligence and provide the necessary coordination in this regard, the “parties” shall share intelligence through mutually agreed secure channels, while observing information security, data protection and confidentiality. Article 10 : Subject to the availability and compatibility of logistical support services, the “parties” shall provide one another with logistical support in peacetime, wartime, and other emergencies, including weapons, ammunition, fuel, spare parts, and other equipment. Article 11 : Without prejudice to international law and the relevant domestic laws of the “parties”, the “parties” shall accept this agreement as the legal basis for implementing its provisions and shall propose additional legal measures where necessary. Article 12 : This agreement shall not prejudice the rights and obligations of the “parties” arising from international agreements they have previously concluded. Article 13: The “parties” shall respect the confidentiality of classified information and documents obtained under this agreement and shall respect national legislation. Classified information and documents shall not be shared with any sta­te, company, or person outside the “parties”. Access to classified information and documents shall be provided on a “need-to-know” basis and only to persons holding the appropriate level of security clearance. Article 14: Any dispute arising from the interpretation or implementation of this agreement shall be settled amicably through consultations and discussions among the “parties”. Article 15: This agreement may be amended through consultations and unanimous agreement among the “core parties”. Article 16: This agreement shall be ratified in accordance with the procedures applicable to each “party” and shall enter into force on the date on which the final instrument of ratification is deposited with the Secretariat of the “Strategic Political and Defence Committee”. This agreement shall remain in force indefinitely. Any “party” may withdraw from this agreement after 10 years have elapsed from its entry into force, by giving the other “parties” written notification of its intention to withdraw through diplomatic channels at least three months in advance. Termination of this agreement or withdrawal from it shall not affect any ongoing activities or projects agreed upon by the “parties” before the date of termination or withdrawal. The responsibilities of the “parties” concerning the protection of classified information and documents and the prevention of their disclosure shall continue after termination of this agreement or withdrawal from it. This agreement has been signed in three original copies in the Turkish, Ar­­­abic, and English languages, each text being equally authentic. In the event of a difference in interpretation between the texts, the English text shall prevail. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Judicial Commission of Pakistan’s transfer-only policy for IHC judges challenged
items.description: ISLAMABAD: A writ petition filed in the Islamabad High Court has challenged the Judicial Commission of Pakistan’s (JCP) April 28 decision that vacancies arising from the transfer of a judge “shall be filled through transfer only”, arguing that the three vacant judges’ seats in the IHC should be filled through fresh appointments under the Constitution rather than further transfers. The petition, filed by Advocate Supreme Court Syed Nayyab Hassan Gardezi against the Federation of Pakistan, JCP, president and prime minister, contends that the impugned decision has no constitutional foundation and conflicts with Article 175A(8), which requires the commission to nominate one person “for each vacancy” of a high court judge. It argues that the Constitution recognises no category of high court vacancy exempt from this requirement and that the commission cannot create one through a resolution. The petition contends that the JCP decision was taken in disregard of the procedure prescribed by the Judicial Commission of Pakistan (Appointment of Judges) Rules 2024. It points out that Rule 11(2) requires the secretary to notify all members at least 14 days before a scheduled meeting, providing the agenda and supporting materials. According to the petition, the impugned decision was reportedly introduced during the proceedings rather than being included in the circulated agenda. It further states that the JCP Rules, as notified, contain no provision for their amendment, while the only provision allowing the commission to remove difficulties — Rule 15 — requires the votes of at least two-thirds of its total membership. The impugned decision, however, records only a “majority of its total membership”. The petition also questions the composition of the JCP when the decision was taken. It argues that the impugned decision governs future appointments to the IHC, yet it was taken at meetings convened to consider transfers, at which the commission sat under the first proviso to Article 200(1), with the chief justices of the high courts concerned in each transfer. By contrast, the Constitution prescribes a distinct composition for the appointment of IHC judges under Article 175A(6). Besides the IHC chief justice, it includes the head of IHC’s constitutional benches, an advocate nominated by the Islamabad Bar Council and a federal minister nominated by the prime minister. The petitioner submits that procedural and compositional defects reinforce the need for the IHC’s three vacancies, created by the transfers notified on April 29, 2026, to be filled through the constitutional process of fresh appointments. For this purpose, nominations should be invited from members of the commission under Article 175A(23) and Rule 9(1) of the JCP Rules, rather than through a transfer-only route. The petition also challenges the decision on grounds of discrimination, retrospectivity and an unlawful fetter on discretion. It notes that in July 2026, the JCP filled vacancies in the Lahore High Court, Sindh High Court and Baloc­histan High Court through initial appointments, while the IHC’s vacancies have been reserved for transfers. It emphasises that the IHC is currently functioning with a chief justice and nine judges against a sanctioned strength of a chief justice and 12 judges, and that the three vacancies have remained unfilled for more than five months. Along with the writ petition, the petitioner has filed an application for interim relief, seeking to restrain the respondents from recommending, advising or notifying the transfer of any judge to the IHC against the three vacancies while the petition remains pending. The petition seeks a declaration that the JCP’s decision is ultra vires Articles 4, 25, 175A and 193 of the Constitution and the JCP Rules, and is of no legal effect. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Makkah alliance binds partners to decade-long pact
items.description: • Turkiye seeks parliamentary nod for defence agreement; officials say Ankara’s support may be limited to provision of weapons, equipment and intelligence sharing • Pakistan has already ratified treaty; only PM and cabinet’s nod required under Article 90 • Egypt’s parliament to vote on support for Riyadh on Oct 26 • Pakistan, Turkiye, Qatar and Indonesia expected to sign defence cooperation agreement in Doha today ANKARA: Turkiye has submitted the Makkah defence pact to parliament for ratification, moving Nato’s second-largest army closer to a formal mutual defence pledge with Riyadh as it continues to face Houthi attacks. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The provision, similar to Nato’s Article 5, refers to Article 51 of the UN Charter, which covers the individual or collective right of states to self-defence against armed attacks. All three members have agreed to use “all necessary means” to eliminate threats to one another’s territorial integrity, sovereignty or internationally recognised borders, as per the text seen by Reuters. The agreement will enter into force upon the deposit of the ratification documents with the secretariat in Riyadh, and will remain valid indefinitely. The parties may not withdraw from the agreement for the first 10 years. While Pakistan has made it clear that ‘collective deterrence measures’ under the trilateral defence agreement are “already in play”, Ankara still requires formal parliamentary ratification for the agreement. According to official sources, Pakistan follows an executive-led treaty-making system, where the federal government’s ratification is enough for subjects in the federal legislative list. According to Article 90 of the Constitution, “the executive authority of the Federation shall be exercised in the name of the President by the Federal Government, consisting of the Prime Minister and the Federal Ministers, which shall act through the Prime Minister, who shall be the chief executive of the Federation.” However, under Tur­kiye’s constitution, separate permission from parliament is required to deploy troops abroad, regardless of any international agreement. According to the Reuters news agency, Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtu­lmus, currently visiting Kyrgyzstan, is expected to refer the agreement to parliament’s foreign affairs commission upon his ret­urn, which could debate the agreement as early as Friday. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s communications director, Burha­nettin Dur­an, said that Turk­iye’s re­cent step marked an important mile­stone towards the institutionalisation of strategic cooperation between the three nations. “This strategic partnership developed between our countries aims to stre­ngthen collective deterrence, enhance joint capabilities in the defence sector, and safeguard security and stability in our region,” Duran said in a post on X. A Turkish official, who spoke to Reuters on the condition of anonymity, said Turkiye’s own contribution was expected to be limited to military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems, adding that no other form of deployment had taken place under the alliance so far. Asked how Turkiye could help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that the Makkah Agree­ment was not an “offensive agreement,” adding that Turkiye would not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory. Although not part of the Makkah alliance, Egypt’s parliament is also expe­cted to vote on authorising pote­ntial military support for Saudi Arabia on Oct 26. Ahead of its submission for parliamentary appr­oval, the contents of the agreement were published in full for the first time by Turkish state broadcaster, TRT Haber. Turkiye, which has a rob­ust defence industry, has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, expressed willingness to help meet Riyadh’s military technology needs and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea. The agreement also envisages close cooperation on defence industry, intelligence sharing, logistical support and the fight against “all means of terrorism,” including at the operational level. Defence deal Meanwhile, TRT World also reported that Turkiye, Qatar, Pakistan and Indonesia are expected to sign a defence industry cooperation memorandum today (Wednesday). The signing will be held in Qatar, which is also expected to announce plans to establish a local defence production hub, the Gulf state’s Minister of State for Defence Affairs Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani told the Global Security Forum in Doha on Monday. Turkish Defence Mini­ster Yasar Guler will travel to Doha for the signing. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, who was also in Doha for the security for­um , is expected to represent Pakistan at the signing. Earlier, Mr Naqvi met with his Qatari counterpart Sheikh Khalifa bin Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, who also commands Qatar’s Internal Security Force (Lekhwiya). The two discussed the current regional situation and matters concerning regional peace and stability, the state-run APP news agency reported. During their meeting, the two men agreed to expand the security partnership between Pakistan and Qatar. They also held detailed discussions on expanding cooperation in areas related to internal security. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Obuasi SHTS: ‘That boundary should not be crossed’ – Safeguarding Lead on students’ food errands
items.description: Ashesi University’s Safeguarding Lead, Dr Millicent Adjei, says asking students to collect food for school authorities crosses a boundary that should protect children from the outset. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, she identified food errands and an environment that discouraged reporting as key safeguarding failures in the Obuasi Senior High Technical School case. Dr Adjei, also Director of International Programs and Campus Cohesion at Ashesi, said the concern began when staff assigned children personal errands. “From what is shared, right from even asking a child entrusted to you to take care of your elderly needs, go to the cafeteria, carry your food for you. That boundary should not be crossed, right?” She said allowing students to take food to the headmaster’s residence represented the first breakdown in protection. Her objection extended to students delivering food elsewhere. “Whether he carried the children to the classroom or wherever, that is a no-no.” Her comments follow Manasseh Azure Awuni’s JoyNews investigation, Inside the Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow . It examines allegations of sexual abuse involving Obuasi SHTS headmaster Zakaria Abdulai. The investigation also documented complaints made to authorities months before his suspension. The Ghana Education Service has interdicted the headmaster pending investigations. A complaint has also been lodged with the police. Dr Adjei said a second failure concerned whether students felt safe enough to report their experiences. “The second level is the environment, the environment that didn’t make it conducive because one of the victims did not feel confident enough or comfortable enough to report, so that enabling environment that allows and empowers them to report was broken.” Referring to the account discussed on the programme, she said a girl’s house prefect had to report the matter. She also cited an account of the girl being hospitalised after being caned, without action being taken. For Dr Adjei, adults entrusted with children must create conditions that encourage them to speak up. “So the second layer, where an environment that doesn’t support speaking up when some of these things happen, was also broken, because when you are given that duty of care, you are supposed to be the protector.” “You are supposed to create that environment where children will be able to come to you, right?”
