items.title: Currency in circulation rises 81% to N5.4trn
items.description: By Peter Egwuatu Currency in circulation in Nigeria rose by 81 per cent to N5.44 trillion in August 2026, from N3.01 trillion in August 2023, underscoring the continued strong demand for physical cash despite the rapid expansion of electronic payments over the past three years. Data from the Central Bank of Nigeria’s, CBN, Money and Credit Statistics show that the strongest increase occurred between August 2023 and August 2024 when currency in circulation rose from N3.010 trillion in August 2023 to N4.55 trillion in August 2024, representing an increase of N1.54 trillion or 51.1 per cent. The growth moderated considerably in the following years. In August 2025, currency in circulation increased to N5.057 trillion, up N508 billion or 11.2 per cent from the previous year. By August 2026, the growth rate moderated further though it hit new threshold of N5.436 trillion, an increase of N379 billion or 7.5 per cent Year-on-Year, YoY. The figures therefore indicate that while the amount of physical cash in circulation has continued to rise, the pace of growth has slowed significantly, from 51.1 per cent in 2024 to 11.2 per cent in 2025 and 7.5 per cent in 2026. Banks’ reserves The increase in currency in circulation occurred alongside a substantial rise in banks’ reserves. According to the data supplied, banks’ reserves rose from N18.528 trillion in August 2023 to N25.456 trillion in August 2024, an increase of N6.928 trillion or 37.4 per cent. They increased further to N31.583 trillion in August 2025, before reaching N36.067 trillion in August 2026. Overall, banks’ reserves increased by N17.539 trillion, or 94.7 per cent, between August 2023 and August 2026. The CBN’s monetary statistics identify currency in circulation and banks’ reserves as components of reserve money or base money. Commenting on the development, David Adonri, Managing Director, High Cap Securities Limited, said: “When more money is held as physical cash, a portion of liquidity is outside the immediate deposit base of commercial banks and is therefore less available for banks to intermediate through loans and other financial assets. However, the rising currency stock should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of excessive liquidity or inflationary pressure. Demand for cash can also increase because of higher nominal prices, larger transaction values and the expansion of economic activity. The increase is particularly noteworthy because Nigeria has experienced rapid growth in electronic payments, mobile banking, fintech services and instant-payment platforms. The continued expansion of physical currency therefore suggests that Nigeria’s digital-payment revolution has not eliminated the country’s cash economy.” Vanguard News The post Currency in circulation rises 81% to N5.4trn appeared first on Vanguard News .

According to Director, the NDC is fully aware of what he described as the desperate and malicious tactics of the APC, which has resorted to offering money, political appointments and other material incentives to induce some money-minded candidates of the party to jump ship and defect to its sinking fold. The statement read: “It has come to the attention of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC, that some candidates of our party have been bribed by the APC to defect to the ruling and ruinous All Progressives Congress, APC, obviously for pecuniary reasons. “The NDC is fully aware of the desperate and malicious tactics of the APC, which has resorted to offering money, political appointments, and other material incentives to induce some money minded candidates of our party to jump ship and defect to its sinking fold. “For those who have fallen for this bait, it is clear that they lack the values, virtues, and ideological commitment associated with our great party. “They were never truly of us. To them, we say good riddance to bad rubbish, and we wish them luck in their political misadventures. “In line with the provisions of the Electoral Act, 2026, the party will immediately conduct fresh congresses to elect credible, competent and trustworthy candidates to replace the defectors in the affected constituency.” “We wish to reassure our teeming party members, supporters, and well-meaning Nigerians not to be perturbed by the antics of the ruling party in bribing a few of our members. These are the last kicks of a dying horse that has seen the handwriting on the wall of its imminent defeat. “NDC remains resolutely committed to its historic mission of rescuing our country from the vice grip of the buccaneers in power and give Nigerians the good governance, security and prosperity they so richly desire. A New Nigeria is POssible. We can do it!” Vanguard News The post Defection of some candidates to APC good riddance to bad rubbish — NDC appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: CDF Munir-Pezeshkian meeting raises peace hopes
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Iranian leaders have told Pakistan that the United States must take the first steps to rebuild trust, and that the acceptance of Tehran’s seven-point proposal could provide a starting point for renewed negotiations. The message was conveyed during Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir’s visit on Tuesday, where he met with President Masoud Pezeshkian, Parliament Speaker Bagher Ghalibaf, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and Mohsen Rezaei, a representative of Iran’s supreme leader and secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi also accompanied the army chief. As diplomatic efforts intensified to prevent a resumption of hostilities, Field Marshal Munir’s visit is being viewed as a move to quell escalating regional tensions. Tehran says acceptance of its 7-point proposal can be starting point for renewed talks with US The visit came a day after Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held talks with Iranian leaders on the conflict and efforts to restore regional stability. The visit was aimed at conveying messages and exploring whether the Islamabad understanding could still provide a basis for negotiations, but no breakthrough or formal agreement was announced after Tuesday’s meetings. The discussions also touched on bilateral relations, including a recent disruption in commercial trade across the Pakistan-Iran border. Iranian officials also raised concerns over the closure, while Field Marshal Munir told them that the border closure was temporary and due to technical reasons and that the crossings had reopened on Tuesday. Importantly, Iranian officials reportedly shared with the field marshal their response to a US proposal, reiterating that Tehran would not make concessions under pressure and that Washington must meet its conditions before trust could be restored. While there was no official word from Pakistan’s Foreign Office or Inter-Services Public Relations, Iranian media described the response as “clear, serious, and explicit”. An Iranian source said the visiting Pakistani army chief was told that “Iran has nothing new to say to the Americans” and it was for them to return to Islamabad Memorandum. Although not many details about President Pezeshkian’s meeting were released to media, in a post that was unrelated to his meeting with Field Marshal Munir, the president said that Iranians may endure hardship, but they will not surrender their land. Speaker Ghalibaf told Field Marshal Munir that the US could not regain Iran’s trust without fulfilling the seven conditions Tehran had presented during meetings in New York. He said Washington’s past actions, including what Iran considers a violation of the Islamabad understanding, had only deepened its distrust of the US administration. “Threats and military manoeuvres cannot influence the strategic decisions of the Islamic Republic of Iran,” Mr Ghalibaf said, according to an Iranian account of the meeting, adding that it was now up to Washington to take the necessary steps to extricate itself from the conflict. Mr Rezaei, meanwhile, said Iran would not surrender its enriched nuclear material, describing it as a national asset intended for domestic use. He said Iranian officials were united in their view that negotiations could not proceed without steps by Washington to meet Tehran’s conditions. The inflexible Iranian response has thrown a challenge for Pakistan, which has sought to revive negotiations between Washington and Tehran after an earlier diplomatic breakthrough failed to produce a lasting settlement. Islamabad brokered a ceasefire in April and hosted direct talks that led to the signing of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in June. The agreement outlined steps towards easing the conflict, reopening the Strait of Hormuz and addressing economic and nuclear issues, but the process subsequently stalled after disagreements. Despite the breakdown of the peace process, Pakistan has continued to offer its good offices to both sides for preventing another round of fighting. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: IMF urges Pakistan to move beyond fiscal targets
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has called for Pakistan’s fiscal policy to go beyond achieving primary balance targets and protecting debt sustainability by reinforcing policy credibility, fostering economic recovery and creating space for public investment and social spending to support stronger long-term growth. Speaking at a workshop on “Reforms for a Modern and Growth-Friendly Tax System in Pakistan”, IMF Middle East and Central Asia Department Director Jihad Azour said tax refo­rm was critical to Pak­is­tan’s economic growth agenda and rema­ined central to the objectives of the Extended Fund Facility (EFF). The workshop was organised by the Ministry of Finance and Revenue in collaboration with the IMF. Finance Minister Muha­mmad Aurangzeb also spoke at the workshop, highlighting achiev­ements over the past two years. Mr Azour said Pakistan had made important progress towards restoring macroeconomic stability, rebuilding confidence, strengthening external buffers and supporting a gradual economic recovery despite an era of shocks and uncertainty. Jihad Azour calls for broader, more predictable tax system The IMF official said Pakistan’s recent stabilisation gains had created an opportunity that needed to be strengthened through transformative reforms, with tax reform at the heart of the process. “A stronger, broader, fairer and more predictable tax system can support fiscal sustainability while reducing distortions that hold back investment, productivity, growth and formal job creation,” he remarked. He said broadening the tax base, strengthening revenue administration, reducing tax expenditures, protecting priority spending and improving public service provision were Pakistan’s priorities. He credited Pakistan for the progress made. However, he said the next milestone was to turn stabilisation into stronger and more durable growth by moving beyond cycles of adjustment towa­r­ds a more competitive, inv­e­s­tment-friendly and inclusive economy. Mr Azour said the IMF remained committed to supporting the authorities in building an economy capable of delivering hig­her productivity, led by a stronger private sector, and creating better opportunities for younger generations. He warned that the highly uncertain external environment had made these objectives more urgent. Fiscal policy, he said, must do more than achieve primary balance targets and protect debt sustainability. It must reinforce policy credibility, foster recovery and create space for public investment and social spending needed to support long-term growth and public welfare. Outlining four themes for discussion during the two-day workshop, Mr Azour identified credibility, growth, fairness and implementation as central to the reform process. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Draft auto policy sent to cabinet
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Tuesday approved the draft Auto Policy 2026-31, which aims to increase auto sector exports to $6 billion and boost local production, competitiveness and electric vehicle (EV) adoption. Although the Prime Minister’s Office did not issue an official statement, sources in the federal government shared the final draft, which was presented to the premier by Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar and Adviser on Industries and Production Haroon Akhtar. The draft policy will be presented to the federal cabinet for in-principle approval, then it will need parliament’s nod. The policy aims to bring the auto sector to open competition by significantly reducing tariffs on completely built-up units (CBUs) and completely knocked-down (CKD) kits up to 15pc by 2030-31. PM ‘okays’ five-year roadmap; policy targets $6bn exports, tariff cuts by 2031; proposes 1pc sales tax on EVs Under the proposed draft, battery electric vehicles will be subject to a 1pc sales tax during 2026-31. The document proposes a 6pc sales tax on range-extended electric vehicles and a 9pc on plug-in hybrid vehicles. A 10pc federal excise duty has been proposed on electric vehicles valued more than $75,000. The policy also envisages lower tariffs on smaller electric vehicles priced below $15,000. To encourage EV adoption, the government has approved proposals to raise the financing limit from Rs3 million to Rs10m and extend the repayment period from three to five years, making smaller vehicles more affordable for low-income consumers. The government has set the total export target of $6.01bn during the five years of the policy, which includes combined exports of parts and vehicles amounting to $256.6m for 2026-27, $671.8m for 2027-28, $1.11bn for 2028-29, $1.17bn for 2029-30 and $2.19bn for 2030-31 the fifth year of the auto policy. The policy also proposes mandatory export targets for vehicle manufacturers, with incentives for companies that increase exports. Under the proposed incentive mechanism, manufacturers would receive compensation equivalent to 5pc of export value for boosting exports, along with an additional 10pc incentive on exports exceeding the previous year’s level. Companies that fail to meet their export targets would face penalties, and manufacturing certificates could be cancelled if targets remain unmet for two consecutive years. The policy also sets new targets to increase the use of locally manufactured auto parts. Companies failing to meet local production targets could lose their incentives. The government expects to collect more than Rs232bn through the Automotive Development Levy over five years. The proceeds would be used to finance export incentives and industrial development programmes, including funding for technology upgrades by auto parts manufacturers. The policy proposes levying the Automotive Development Levy on vehicles with engine capacities exceeding 1,000cc. To strengthen quality assurance and regulatory oversight, the government plans to establish the Pakistan Automotive Testing Institute. The policy also provides funding for research, certification, and third-party audits, as well as the adoption of international safety standards for locally manufactured and imported vehicles. Meanwhile, Pakistan Association of Automotive Parts and Accessories Manufacturers (Paapam) Chairman Abdul Rehman Aizaz said the new policy, by lowering the import tariff on parts to 15pc, would phase out local parts manufacturers and benefit assemblers, warning that assemblers could eventually be phased out as imported cars take over.“This policy will make Pakistan an import destination country with no local industrial base in the auto sector,” he remarked. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: State of deceased’s eyes not proof of ‘unwitnessed’ death: SC
items.description: • Court dismisses petitions challenging double-murder convictions • Verdict explains that closing eyes of a corpse is ‘religious’ custom, not legal duty ISLAMABAD: The Supreme Court ruled on Tuesday that the condition of a deceased person’s eyes at the time of death cannot conclusively establish the fact that the incident was not witnessed. The Qanun-i-Shahadat Order, 1984, does not impose a legal duty to close a deceased person’s eyes. Rather, the practice is customary and religious, observed Justice Salahuddin Panhwar while dismissing jail petitions filed by Azmat Ullah alias Motu and Muhammad Luqman alias Gona. The petitioners had challenged their convictions in a 2011 double-murder case, upheld by the Lahore High Court (LHC) on May 18, 2022. Justice Panhwar was part of a three-member bench, headed by Justice Muhammad Hashim Khan Kakar. The bench upheld the convictions under Section 302(b) of the Pakistan Penal Code but maintained the high court’s decision to commute the death sentences to life imprisonment. In criminal trials, defence lawyers often argue that an incident was ‘unwitnessed’ if the post-mortem report records the deceased’s eyes as open, reasoning that close relatives would ordinarily close them after death. During the hearing, the petitioners’ counsel pointed to discrepancies in eyewitness statements and argued that the post-mortem and inquest reports, which recorded the eyes of both victims as open, indicated that the murders had not been witnessed. Article 129 versus rigid presumptions In a nine-page judgement, Justice Panhwar referred to Article 129 of the Qanun-i-Shahadat Order, which allows courts to presume facts they consider likely in the circumstances of a particular case. However, the judgement stressed that human behaviour could not be assessed in a vacuum or through rigid assumptions. Responses to trauma, terror and violent loss vary from person to person, making it unsafe to draw categorical conclusions from a single circumstance. It noted that relatives witnessing a gruesome incident may be overwhelmed by shock and trauma. Hoping their loved one might survive, they may focus on obtaining urgent medical assistance rather than performing customary rituals associated with death. Relatives and bystanders may also continue treating the victim as injured until a doctor or police official confirms death, which may not be immediately apparent at the scene. Other factors From a forensic perspective, the position of the eyelids is governed by physiological processes rather than the presence or absence of witnesses, the judgement explained. Following death, muscles initially become relaxed, allowing eyelids to remain open or partially open, a condition known as lagophthalmos. Handling or moving a body may also cause previously closed eyes to reopen, particularly before rigor mortis develops. As rigor mortis sets in, muscles become stiff and retain their prevailing position. The court also cited Locard’s Exchange Principle, which holds that every contact leaves a trace. Relatives, bystanders and rescue workers may avoid touching a body to prevent contamination or disturbance of blood-spatter patterns, trace evidence and DNA material before forensic experts arrive. It would therefore be unsafe to presume that every person knows how to handle a deceased body or feels obliged to close the eyes, the judgement said. Concluding that neither forensic literature nor the law recognises closed eyes as an indicator of a witnessed death, the court rejected the argument that open eyelids alone could establish that a crime was unwitnessed. The judgement further observed that minor discrepancies and natural variations in eyewitness accounts, arising from the passage of time and the rigours of cross-examination, do not undermine otherwise credible and consistent testimony. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: Balochistan says Rs14bn spent to counter terrorism
items.description: • Insists 18 laws enacted, 17 institutions set up under security plans • Officials claim 60,000 operations conducted, 1,100 terrorists killed QUETTA: The Balochistan government has passed 18 laws, established 17 institutions and departments and spent more than Rs14 billion on counterterrorism measures under the National Action Plan, Counterterrorism Policy and Provincial Action Plan, senior provincial officials said on Tuesday. They also claimed that more than 60,000 counterterrorism operations had been conducted across Balochistan up to October, killing over 1,000 terrorists. The Counter-Terrorism Depart­ment alone had killed 250 terrorists and arrested another 250 suspects. They said 101 police personnel and around 200 members of other law enforcement agencies had lost their lives, while 551 civilians had been killed in terrorist violence. The figures were revealed during a joint press conference held by Provincial Home Minister Ziaullah Langove along with Chief Mini­ster’s Adviser on Media and Political Aff­a­irs Shahid Rind and Additional Chief Secretary Home Hamza Shafqaat. They said measures had also been taken to secure the Quetta-Rakhni, Quetta-Karachi and Quetta-Taftan highways and expressed confidence that the security situation would improve over the next three to four months. Mr Shafqaat said the provincial government had taken a series of measures over the past two years to implement the National Action Plan, Counter Terrorism Policy and Provincial Action Plan. Published in Dawn, October 21st, 2026

items.title: ‘Some teachers fight male students over schoolgirls’ — Teacher alleges
items.description: A teacher at Ekumpoano Catholic Basic School, Stephen Desu, has alleged that some teachers in senior high schools compete with male students for the attention of female students and punish boys who attempt to get close to the girls. He said the alleged conduct reflected a disturbing abuse of authority in schools, where teachers entrusted with students’ welfare could use their positions to intimidate those they were supposed to guide and protect. “It’s like sometimes they are fighting male students over the girls they are interested in,” Mr Desu said on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, October 20. “Yes, over girls in the schools. And if you try to get close to those girls, those teachers will punish you, punish you till you leave those girls alone,” he added. His comments came amid national concern over allegations of sexual abuse involving female students at Obuasi Senior High Technical School (SHTS), where headmaster Zakaria Abdulai has been interdicted by the Ghana Education Service (GES) and arrested by the police as investigations continue. The case has attracted widespread attention following reports by JoyNews investigative correspondent Manasseh Azure Awuni. ‘The problem is worse at SHS level’ Mr Desu said sexual misconduct in schools was not limited to senior high schools, but argued that the problem was more pronounced at that level. “At the primary level, the problem is there. At the JHS level, it’s there. But it’s worse. It’s worse at the SHS level,” he said. He further alleged that some teachers actively sought postings to senior high schools because of opportunities to engage in sexual misconduct. “And almost every school, if all of us will be politically correct with everything, everybody is aware that almost every school, there is one or there are two teachers who are engaged in this,” he said. Mr Desu urged the public to take concerns about teacher misconduct seriously, suggesting that former students, particularly women, could provide accounts of inappropriate behaviour they had witnessed or experienced. His comments raise questions about how schools address allegations of sexual exploitation, protect students from intimidation and ensure that teachers do not misuse their authority. The allegations surrounding Obuasi SHTS have intensified scrutiny of the systems for reporting and investigating sexual misconduct in schools. Mr Desu’s account points to concerns that students may be vulnerable not only to inappropriate conduct but also to retaliation when they attempt to form relationships or challenge the behaviour of adults in positions of authority.

items.title: Cornell Jane Doe says embattled university head doubted her gang-rape allegation
items.description: A former Cornell student who alleges she was gang-raped at a fraternity house has said she felt “unsupported and disbelieved” by the university president. Known only as Jane Doe, she wrote a letter accusing President Michael Kotlikoff of asking why she waited several weeks to report the incident. The Ivy League institution in upstate New York says her account of the Cornell head’s reaction is “incorrect”. She addressed her letter to campus faculty who will vote this month on Kotlikoff’s leadership in a rare vote. Doe filed her lawsuit last month alleging she was raped by several men in October 2024 at a Chi Phi fraternity party. All seven former fraternity members Doe accused have denied wrongdoing when the BBC’s US partner, CBS, contacted them. None has been charged with a crime. Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police, and the local prosecutor declined to bring charges at the time, but the case has since reopened . In response to Doe’s initial allegation, Cornell said it opened an internal investigation and a civil rights inquiry. In a two-page letter dated 14 October and obtained by the BBC, Doe told the faculty senate that after she reported the alleged rape, she received “a second-hand account” of Kotlikoff’s reaction and that his “initial response” was “along the lines of, ‘Why did she wait so long to report it?'” Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police on 8 November, about three weeks after the fraternity party. She noted that Kotlikoff had a conversation with the then-president of her sorority and that other staff members were present, at least one of whom “appeared distressed” by the college president’s question. Doe said in her letter: “It diminished my confidence in the administration’s ability to approach my experience with the understanding, sensitivity, and fairness I had hoped for and expected from what had been my dream school.” She said she wrote the letter so that faculty “can make an informed choice” ahead of their 28 October vote on whether to express no confidence in Kotlikoff’s leadership. The university confirmed receipt of the letter from Doe’s lawyer. But in a statement to the BBC, a Cornell spokesperson said: “The second-hand account of the question asked by President Kotlikoff in a January 2025 meeting in the letter is incorrect, based on a documented first-hand account.” The spokesperson said Kotlikoff’s question about the delay in reporting the alleged rape “was directed at bystanders who did not use Cornell’s anonymous tip line, despite ongoing social media activity about the incident in October 2024”. “He was not questioning Jane Doe’s reporting,” the spokesperson said. Kotlikoff, who has led the Ithaca-based institution for 26 years, was grilled by the faculty senate last Wednesday. Staff said they were “deeply disturbed” by his handling of the case and accused him of lacking an “emotional response”, according to recordings obtained by the BBC. Kotlikoff highlighted changes the university had introduced as a result of Doe’s allegations, including banning fraternity parties. “We are all extraordinarily upset by the events at Cornell in October of 2024,” he said. The faculty senate, a governing body composed of professors and other academic staff at Cornell, scheduled their no-confidence vote for 28 October. In recordings of the meeting, faculty said sexual misconduct on campus was a systemic problem that demanded “systemic attention”. Paul Ortiz, a labour history professor who sponsored the no-confidence resolution, said students had told faculty they “feel unsafe walking to the library after dark”. He accused Cornell of treating rape “as more of a ‘PR problem’ than a heinous crime”.

items.title: France to deploy military forces for next protests
items.description: France will deploy troops from its counterterrorism military forces to support police and gendarmes ahead of demonstrations expected on October 24, the government said on Tuesday, acknowledging failures in its response to last weekend's violence. Speaking in the National Assembly, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said the troops would mainly serve in static security roles, allowing police and gendarmes to focus on mobile law enforcement and respond more flexibly to potential violence. He told lawmakers that the security forces deployed on October 17 had been "not mobile enough." The government is also considering banning unauthorized demonstrations, as well as officially declared protests deemed at risk of spiraling out of control, Nunez said. "The deployment next Saturday will be massive," Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said, adding that the immediate priority was to restore order after rioting and looting swept Paris, Marseille, Lyon and other cities at the weekend. Lecornu acknowledged shortcomings in the state's response at the weekend, saying there had been intelligence failures, while police deployments had been too static and authorities had erred by not cancelling planned police leave. France saw nationwide protests on October 17, with the government estimating that around 550,000 people took part, while organizers put the figure at 800,000. Some demonstrations were marred by violent clashes. According to official figures, at least 3,000 shops were looted nationwide. Some trade unions and student groups have set November 5 as the date for another nationwide protest. Meanwhile, some activists who took part in the October 17 demonstrations have called for further protests on October 24. Parliament is setting up a commission of inquiry to establish the causes of the unrest, while authorities have assigned 200 ​investigators to identify and track down those involved in the street violence. Police arrested on Tuesday a man suspected of starting a blaze that destroyed a historic town hall in the central city of Limoges during the rioting. Officials said he had been on a security watch list and belonged to an ultra-left group. A night of relative ‌calm in France followed targeted curfews imposed in several areas on Monday affected by the chaos, which the government said had helped reassert control. The localized curfews, some directed at children and teenagers under age 18, were extended to Tuesday night, police said. (With input from agencies)

items.title: FG confirms Ebola case in FCT, begins contact tracing
items.description: By Chidinma Chukwu, Abuja The Federal Government has reportedly commenced contact tracing after a suspected imported case of Ebola disease was identified in the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), with 44 close contacts said to have been identified. The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate, was quoted as disclosing this in a statement signed by the ministry’s Assistant Director of Information and Public Relations, Ado Bako, following the reported laboratory confirmation on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. According to the statement, the patient is a woman who recently arrived in Nigeria on an international flight from Uganda. The woman was reportedly admitted to a private hospital in the FCT, where she received treatment for several days before the diagnosis was confirmed. She is said to be in isolation and receiving medical care. Pate said the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the FCT Health Services Secretariat and other relevant authorities were working together to contain the reported infection. He said contact tracing had commenced, with public health teams identifying and monitoring people who might have been exposed to the virus. Those being monitored reportedly include healthcare workers, patients, caregivers and people who may have come into contact with the patient during her travels. The statement also said surveillance had been intensified, while the hospital where the patient was treated was receiving support to strengthen infection prevention and control measures. The minister urged people contacted during the tracing exercise, including relevant airline passengers, to provide the necessary information and comply with public health advice. He also called on public and private healthcare facilities nationwide to remain vigilant and promptly report suspected cases to public health authorities. Healthcare workers were advised to maintain a high index of suspicion, identify and isolate suspected cases without delay, and observe strict infection prevention and control measures. The government urged Nigerians to remain calm and vigilant, practise regular hand hygiene and avoid contact with the body fluids of anyone suspected of having Ebola. Symptoms to watch for include fever, severe weakness, headache, vomiting and diarrhoea, particularly among people who may have been exposed to the virus. Pate advised anyone who suspected exposure to contact public health authorities immediately, even if they had no symptoms. He also urged anyone who developed symptoms to avoid close contact with others and call public health authorities for guidance before visiting a healthcare facility. The minister warned against spreading rumours or stigmatising people who might have been exposed, urging Nigerians to rely on verified information from official health authorities. He said the Federal Government, FCT authorities and their partners were working to protect healthcare workers, patients and the wider public, adding that investigations were ongoing. The statement said the NCDC’s toll-free call centre was available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, to provide information and receive reports of suspected cases. Members of the public were advised to call 6232 for assistance. Vanguard Newspaper The post FG confirms Ebola case in FCT, begins contact tracing appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Migrants à Sebta : La justice appelée à enquêter sur des violences présumées de militaires espagnols
items.description: Le quotidien espagnol El País appelle à l’ouverture d’une enquête judiciaire urgente sur des agressions présumées commises par des militaires espagnols contre des migrants entrés à l'enclave occupée de Sebta les 30 et 31 juillet, lors d’une crise migratoire qui avait vu affluer quelque 70.000 personnes depuis le Maroc. Dans son éditorial publié mardi, le journal estime que des rapports médicaux transmis à la justice constituent désormais des éléments suffisants pour faire la lumière sur ces accusations. Au nombre d’une vingtaine environ, ces documents ont été adressés par l’hôpital universitaire de Sebta au tribunal de la ville. Ils font état de blessures dont auraient souffert des migrants après avoir été frappés par des soldats espagnols participant aux patrouilles de sécurité. Pour El País , ces éléments justifient l’ouverture d’investigations judiciaires afin de vérifier les faits et d’établir les éventuelles responsabilités. Le quotidien considère que ces rapports médicaux renforcent la crédibilité d’accusations apparues à la suite de l’afflux migratoire des 30 et 31 juillet. Des vidéos et des photographies diffusées sur les réseaux sociaux et relayées par les médias avaient alors fait état de violences indiscriminées contre des migrants, imputées à des individus en uniforme espagnol. Des témoignages et des enregistrements au cœur du dossier Ces accusations avaient également été documentées par Amnesty International. Dans un rapport publié en septembre dernier, l’organisation de défense des droits humains a recensé des actes de torture ainsi que d’autres traitements cruels, inhumains ou dégradants qui auraient été infligés à des migrants par des membres de la Légion espagnole et du régiment régulier de Sebta. Le document s’appuie notamment sur 22 témoignages détaillés et des photographies montrant les blessures des victimes. Amnesty International a toutefois choisi de préserver leur anonymat afin de garantir leur sécurité. Le dossier comporte également des enregistrements audio divulgués dans les médias. Le 15 septembre 2026, le ministère espagnol de la Défense les a transmis au tribunal de Sebta et au parquet. Ces enregistrements font entendre des soldats, supposés être stationnés dans la ville, se vanter sur un ton moqueur d’avoir frappé des migrants et de les avoir maltraités. L’absence de données permettant d’identifier les victimes a cependant constitué un obstacle majeur au déroulement de la procédure judiciaire, souligne El País . Le quotidien estime que les rapports médicaux transmis à la justice pourraient permettre de surmonter en partie cette difficulté en apportant des éléments objectifs sur les blessures constatées. Une obligation d’enquête pour les autorités Pour le journal espagnol, le tribunal dispose désormais de suffisamment d’éléments pour déterminer si les blessures consignées dans les documents médicaux résultent effectivement d’actes commis par des soldats espagnols. Il rappelle que le droit international humanitaire impose aux États d’ouvrir d’office une enquête lorsque des indices font apparaître des soupçons de mauvais traitements ou de torture imputables à des agents publics. Cette obligation, estime El País , s’applique pleinement à l’affaire de Sebta. L’enjeu est désormais de vérifier les accusations, de déterminer les circonstances des faits allégués et, le cas échéant, d’établir les responsabilités individuelles. Le quotidien conclut qu’une enquête rapide et effective serait dans l’intérêt de toutes les parties, y compris des forces armées espagnoles. Il met en garde contre le risque de laisser croire que de tels comportements pourraient être tolérés et appelle les autorités à exercer la plus grande vigilance pour garantir le respect intégral des obligations découlant du droit international. The post Migrants à Sebta : La justice appelée à enquêter sur des violences présumées de militaires espagnols appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: At Bawku Senior High, a headmaster returns to the trees he planted as a student
items.description: Some of the trees shading Bawku Senior High School were planted by Reverend Abugbilla Bukari and his fellow students. Bukari arrived at the school in 1991. The following year, the headmaster who admitted him, the late B.J.L. Kumasi, led students in planting trees for what became known as the Kumasi Woodlot. Bukari said it was the school’s first deliberate effort to establish a woodlot on campus since it was founded in 1963. “I still remember some of the trees I personally planted,” he said. “They are standing today as a testament to the work we did under his leadership.” The effort brought the school national recognition. In 1992, it received a national tree-planting award, Bukari recalled. He remembers the celebration that followed, with truckloads of rice, cooking oil and sardines arriving, and the students were fed for nearly a month. More than three decades later, Bukari returned to Bawku SHS as its substantive headmaster in 2024. He saw the appointment as a chance to continue the tradition that had shaped his own appreciation of trees. That year, students and staff, led by the Agriculture Department, planted 480 Acacia trees on campus. The school says 450 have survived, a survival rate of about 94 per cent. “It is a wonderful feeling,” Bukari said of standing under trees he helped plant as a student. The older trees provide shade and fresh air and have beautified the school, he said. He hopes students who leave Bawku SHS will return decades from now and find that the number of trees has grown. Students learn by planting The 2024 planting gave students a chance to take part directly in establishing the new trees and to consider what trees contribute to their school. A final-year agriculture student, Ahmed Faizatu Akudugu, said the trees create places for recreation and help make the campus more comfortable. “They provide spaces for recreation, beautify the school environment and help regulate temperatures on the campus,” she said. Another student also in an agriculture class, Asianib Elizabeth Apoasaan, said she was excited to take part. “We planted the trees for several reasons. First, they provide spaces for recreation. Second, they contribute to efforts to address climate change by helping to improve the environment,” she said. Apoasaan thanked the headmaster for encouraging the programme and said she hoped future students would value the trees. “We hope that students who come after us will also appreciate and learn from what we have started,” she said. Head of the school’s Agriculture Department, Awini Bashiru Issah, said students gain practical knowledge by taking part in the work. “The students contribute labour to the exercise, but, more importantly, they gain practical experience in planting trees. They learn by doing, which helps them understand the process and appreciate its importance,” he said. Issah said schools have a role in preparing young people to continue that work. “They are the generation that will take over from us, and we must equip them with the knowledge, practical skills and commitment to continue planting and protecting trees for the benefit of future generations,” he said. A school planting in Ghana’s national tree-growing effort Bawku SHS planted in 2024, the same year Ghana held its fourth Green Ghana Day. The government launched the Green Ghana Project in 2021 to encourage tree planting and help restore forest cover. The 2024 national target was 10 million seedlings; the Forestry Commission later reported distributing about 13.9 million seedlings for planting. The government has continued that restoration drive through the Tree for Life Reforestation Initiative, launched in 2025 to restore degraded landscapes, including areas affected by deforestation and illegal mining. The Information Services Department reported that the programme planted about 31 million seedlings in 2025 and restored approximately 23,600 hectares. Bawku SHS’s experience shows what the national effort depends on at the local level: students and staff planting trees, the school caring for them, and practical protection to help them grow. The climate value and the limits of planting Trees absorb carbon dioxide as they grow and store carbon in their trunks, branches and roots. On a school campus, they also provide shade and can make outdoor spaces more comfortable. Bawku SHS students say the trees help regulate campus temperatures and improve the grounds. Those benefits matter in a country facing rising temperatures and changing rainfall patterns. The Ghana Meteorological Agency’s Climate Atlas projects that Ghana’s average annual temperature will rise by about 1.5 degrees Celsius by the end of the century under its RCP 4.5 scenario. The agency also projects seasonal rainfall changes, even as total annual rainfall is expected to remain broadly stable. Tree planting alone cannot reverse climate change. Location, species, and follow-up care matter, too. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change says reforestation can support climate mitigation and ecosystem functions, while poorly planned projects can harm biodiversity, water security and other local priorities. At Bawsco, all 480 trees planted in the recent exercise are Acacia. Their survival is an encouraging early measure. Authorities say continued monitoring will show whether they thrive through changing seasons and what care they need. Protecting the woodlot Bukari said livestock sometimes enter the school grounds and threaten the young trees. “In about two to three months, the surrounding vegetation will become bare, and animals will be attracted to the green trees on our campus. They may feed on or damage them,” he said. The school is seeking a perimeter wall. Bukari said GETFund officials measured the proposed wall at about 3.29 kilometres and awarded a contract. He appealed for the work to proceed: “The project requires government support. A contract has been awarded, but I am appealing through your media platform for the contractor to move to the site and complete the work to the required standard.” “The wall will help protect the trees, as well as lives and property within the school,” he said. Bukari is also concerned about what forest loss could mean for the school’s future fuel supply. “If the current trend continues, we may struggle to find enough trees for firewood in the future,” he said. He hopes the woodlot can be managed sustainably and help provide fuel for the school kitchen when needed, alongside a transition to biogas and other alternatives. He sees the planting effort as part of a responsibility shared across Ghana. “Our efforts are not only for Bawku Senior High School. We see tree planting as a national responsibility,” he said. He believes the country’s more than 700 senior high and technical schools could help grow the next generation of trees. Bukari hopes students who leave Bawku SHS will return in 30 years and find the number of trees has grown significantly.

items.title: Can Tinubu campaign without campaigning?
items.description: By LANRE OGUNDIPE There is something intriguing about President Bola Tinubu’s approach to the 2027 presidential campaign. He appears determined not to conduct the election as though the business of governing Nigeria can be suspended for the sake of campaigning. Rather than carry his campaign physically from one rally to another, he is placing considerable responsibility on governors, party officials, ministers, legislators and political allies to take the message into the country. At first glance, this could look like a candidate stepping back from the electorate. I see something more calculated. Tinubu may be testing whether the political organisation he has spent decades building is now strong enough to campaign on his behalf. That is the real question. The 2027 election may be the first major test of whether Tinubu can turn a presidential campaign from a candidate-centred operation into a system-wide political enterprise. If he can, it would say something important about the sophistication of his political organisation. But it would also expose the limit of political engineering: an organisation can carry a message into every state, but it cannot determine whether citizens believe the message. Tinubu is not an accidental politician. He has spent decades learning the mechanics of power, from the difficult years of opposition politics to the construction of the Lagos political machine, the coalition that eventually became the APC, the struggle against an incumbent federal government and, finally, the presidency. He understands something many politicians learn too late: a serious political organisation cannot depend entirely on the physical presence of one man. The APC’s latest campaign structure suggests that this is precisely the calculation. The revised presidential campaign council places all 32 APC governors in charge of the presidential campaign in their respective states. It also reaches beyond the APC itself, assigning campaign responsibilities to Nyesom Wike in Rivers and the Federal Capital Territory, Chukwuma Soludo in Anambra and Ademola Adeleke in Osun. Tinubu remains at the centre of the structure, with Vice President Kashim Shettima and APC national chairman Nentawe Yilwatda as his principal deputies. This is more than a distribution of campaign duties. It is an attempt to make the campaign a network rather than a procession behind one candidate. The President governs from Abuja. Governors take the political argument into the states. Ministers defend the administration. Legislators mobilise their constituencies. Party officials coordinate the structure. Political allies outside the APC widen the coalition. Tinubu is effectively asking whether the political system he has assembled can do much of the campaigning traditionally expected of the presidential candidate himself. There is historical precedent for such an approach, but the lesson from history is more nuanced than the simple proposition that delegation works. Richard Nixon’s 1972 re-election offers the closest parallel. His campaign allowed him to spend substantial time governing while surrogates carried the message across the country, and he went on to win 49 of 50 states. But the organisation worked because it was operating in a favourable political environment. Jimmy Carter’s defeat in 1980 showed the reverse. His limited campaigning during the Iran hostage crisis was only one element in an election already shaped by economic dissatisfaction, political fatigue and Ronald Reagan’s challenge. Four years later, Reagan benefited from an improving economy that allowed his record to become a powerful campaign argument in its own right. Nigeria has its own cautionary history. Shehu Shagari’s 1983 re-election demonstrated the reach of incumbency and party organisation, but the controversy surrounding that election remains a reminder that political strength and democratic legitimacy are not interchangeable. The lesson is simple: political organisation can amplify a favourable political environment. It cannot manufacture one. That is where the Nigerian reality becomes decisive for Tinubu. A governor can explain the administration’s reforms. A minister can defend its policy choices. Party officials can mobilise supporters and political allies can broaden the coalition. But Nigerians will not assess the 2027 election solely through political speeches. They will also assess it through the cost of feeding their families, moving to work, paying rent, keeping the lights on, sending children to school and dealing with insecurity. This is where public hardship deserves careful treatment. Hardship is politically powerful, but it is not politically deterministic. Nigerians can endure painful reforms if they believe the pain is temporary, necessary and producing visible results. They can also reject an administration that tells them the future will be better when their experience of the present offers little evidence of improvement. The real political question, therefore, is not whether Nigerians have suffered. They plainly have. It is whether enough Nigerians will believe that the suffering is producing a destination worth reaching. That is why the President’s own argument about reform matters. Tinubu has repeatedly maintained that Nigerians have endured necessary sacrifices and that the foundations for a stronger economy are being laid. He has also acknowledged the crucial next step: the benefits of reform must increasingly be felt in the daily lives of ordinary Nigerians. By 2027, that will no longer be merely an economic argument. It will be an electoral proposition. Are Nigerians better off? The answer will not be determined by how convincingly the governors explain the reforms. Nor will it be determined simply by how angry critics are about them. It will be determined by whether citizens can see and feel enough improvement to conclude that the sacrifice was worth it. If food becomes more affordable, transport less punishing, electricity more reliable, security stronger, jobs more available and purchasing power better, the administration’s record may begin to campaign for itself. The governors and other surrogates would then have something much stronger than a talking point. They would have lived evidence. But if household hardship remains stubbornly dominant, the political calculation becomes much harder. A government can have respectable macroeconomic indicators and still struggle to persuade citizens who cannot reconcile those indicators with the arithmetic of their homes. That is not necessarily proof that the reforms have failed. It is proof that economic reform and political legitimacy do not always move at the same speed. This is where Tinubu’s political sophistication will face its most serious test. Governors are not merely campaign operatives. They are politicians with their own futures, successors to produce, factions to manage, alliances to preserve and political debts to repay. Their interests may overlap with Tinubu’s, but they are not identical to his. The deployment of 32 governors therefore gives the ruling party extraordinary political reach while simultaneously creating a complex web of state-level calculations. Tinubu’s long political apprenticeship becomes significant here. His political strength has arguably never rested principally on speechmaking. It has rested on political engineering: building coalitions, identifying useful alliances, accommodating competing interests and keeping a broad political structure together long enough to achieve an objective. The inclusion of politicians outside the APC can therefore be understood as an extension of that philosophy. The coalition is less about ideological purity than electoral arithmetic. That is politics as Tinubu has practised it for decades. But political sophistication carries a danger of its own. Those who command a political structure can begin to confuse the strength of their organisation with the strength of their argument. The 2027 electorate will not be a meeting of governors. It will be millions of individual decisions. A voter may cheer at a rally and vote differently. He may support the direction of the reforms but dislike their consequences. He may believe that the sacrifice is finally producing results. Or he may conclude that he has sacrificed enough. Those decisions cannot be read reliably from the size of a crowd, the number of governors behind a candidate or the prominence of the people assembled on a campaign platform. This is why Tinubu does not necessarily need to be everywhere. But he needs to be present where the political argument is most difficult. He needs to explain the choices his government has made, defend its record, answer its critics and, above all, demonstrate that he understands the distance between a reform that looks successful on a government balance sheet and one that feels successful in a Nigerian household. That may ultimately determine whether his unconventional campaign strategy becomes a masterstroke or a miscalculation. If the political environment is improving, the governors can amplify it. If citizens are beginning to feel relief, the campaign can give that relief a political narrative. If hardship remains the dominant experience, however, political organisation will have a much harder task. It can explain hardship. It can ask for patience. It can present the promise of tomorrow. It cannot erase the experience of today. The machine can carry the message. It cannot determine whether Nigerians believe it. That is the real test of Tinubu’s 2027 strategy. And when the campaign finally gives way to the ballot, the most carefully constructed political architecture in the country will still have to confront the one variable it cannot organise away: the independent judgement of the Nigerian voter. •Ogundipe, a public affairs analyst, wrote in from Abuja. items.title: Nigerians demand relief, not mere figures
items.description: President Bola Tinubu can point to credible evidence that Nigeria’s economy is stabilising. The World Bank says GDP grew by 4.2 per cent in the first half of 2026, against 3.9 per cent a year earlier, and projects average growth of 4.4 per cent through 2028. Inflation, which fell during 2025, has faced renewed pressure from higher fuel and transport costs. External reserves and public revenues have strengthened. World Trade Organisation (WTO) Director-General, Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, credited Tinubu’s administration in 2025 for stabilising the economy. She stressed that the next tasks were growth, job creation and social safety nets. But stability is a foundation for prosperity, not prosperity itself. Tinubu’s government has taken difficult measures: implementing petrol subsidy removal, partially removing electricity subsidies, liberalising the naira and pursuing tax reforms. They have eased fiscal pressures, improved foreign exchange conditions and increased revenue available to governments. The World Bank says growth has stabilised for the first time since 2019. Yet the public’s experience remains harsh. Astronomically higher petrol and electricity costs feed into transport, food production and household bills. Naira depreciation made imports and production inputs more expensive, while wages have struggled to keep pace. Millions face difficult choices over food, rent, medicines and school fees. This explains resentment towards the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) in many communities: people endure sacrifices but see too little relief. In his Independence Day address, Tinubu declared the onset of an “era of prosperity”, suggesting the next four years would reward Nigerians’ pain if he wins another term in 2027. But trust must be earned. Citizens are unlikely to believe promises while political office-holders appear insulated from hardship. The contrast is sharpened by conspicuous official spending. In June 2026, a Federal High Court declared unlawful the National Assembly’s N110 billion spending on 465 sport-utility vehicles and lawmakers’ support allowances, citing breaches of procurement rules and public trust. Expensive presidential operations, travels and budgeted vehicle spending for senior officials and judicial officers deepen the perception that austerity is only for ordinary people. Public institutions must justify such expenditure transparently, especially when schools and hospitals remain underfunded. The government’s 30-day NNPC petrol-price relief is welcome but temporary. Tinubu should publish an audited account of reform savings and spending, expand transport support, protect basic electricity consumers, and prioritise food production, major federal roads, healthcare and education. The government should enforce transparent procurement, cut non-essential travel, fleets and luxury refurbishments, and ensure wages keep pace with living costs. States must justify higher revenues and protect the poorest and most vulnerable households. The World Bank’s figures offer cautious hope, not a certificate of success. Prosperity will be measured in affordable meals, decent jobs, reliable power and functioning public services. Only Nigerians can validate claims of credible economic performance. The post Nigerians demand relief, not mere figures appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Goudomp : un jeune poignardé à mort lors d’un entraînement de football, le suspect arrêté
items.description: Une banale dispute a viré au drame sur un terrain d’entraînement de football à Goudomp. Alphousseyni Gassama a perdu la vie après avoir reçu un coup de couteau porté par l’un de ses camarades, identifié comme Charles Nzalé. Après les faits, le suspect présumé a pris la fuite en direction de la Guinée-Bissau. Il a finalement été intercepté par les forces de sécurité dans la commune frontalière de Ngore. Ce drame plonge la communauté de Goudomp dans la consternation et la tristesse. S. DIAMANKA

items.title: Obuasi SHTS: Food errands to staff homes are a safeguarding red flag – Safeguarding Officer
items.description: Safeguarding Officer at Kingsdale Secondary Schools in the UK, Amartei K. Amartey, says sending female students to deliver food to staff homes is itself a safeguarding breach. Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said the practice left students vulnerable. It also undermined safeguards intended to protect staff. “Why is a girl child carrying food to a staff member’s house? That’s a safeguarding issue. That’s a red flag,” he said. His comments follow allegations of sexual abuse at Obuasi Senior High Technical School. Manasseh Azure Awuni’s investigation, Inside the Dreaded Headmaster’s Bungalow , examines allegations against headmaster Zakaria Abdulai. It also documents complaints made to authorities months before his suspension. The Ghana Education Service has interdicted the headmaster pending investigations. A complaint has also been lodged with the police. For Mr Amartey, the food errands raised a fundamental concern that should have demanded action on its own. “That action of asking a female student to carry your food from the dining hall to your house—that alone, you must go.” Asked whether a teacher in the UK could send a child from the dining hall to their residence with food, he replied: “Never. You won’t even dream about it.” He argued that safeguarding rules exist to prevent situations that leave children vulnerable. Observing those boundaries also protects staff when accounts of an encounter are disputed. “Because the girl child found herself in a vulnerable place. The teacher or staff member claims they are innocent. What is their evidence?” He questioned why a staff member would breach the very rules designed to protect both parties. “Why have you broken the number one rule, which is safeguarding—not just safeguarding for the child, but for you, the member of staff as well.” Mr Amartey also criticised the committee’s handling of the matter. He said the safeguarding concern was already clear from the decision to send a girl to a staff member’s home. “For me, it’s just been a waste of time.” He maintained that following safeguarding rules was central to avoiding conflicting accounts of what happened. “And you broke the rule. So for me, it shouldn’t even go beyond this.”

items.title: The Supreme Court and national interest: The judiciary as a public-policy institution (2), by Usman Sarki
items.description: “The essence of federalism is full mutual consent. ” — John Buchan Recalling Nigeria’s history in this discourse matters because the country is not an ordinary political community or mere contraption, as some advocates of restructuring erroneously imagine. It comprises peoples of deep consciousness, immense diversity in language, religion, culture, historical experience and political organisation, who expect these differences to coexist peacefully and equally within one sovereign state under one supreme legal framework. The country’s unity cannot be sustained by geographical reference, rhetoric, agitations, coercion or sentiment alone. It must rest upon a continuing constitutional bargain in which citizens and constituent units trust that rights will be respected, powers bounded and regularised, and disputes peacefully resolved. This is where I suppose John Buchan’s reflections on federation become relevant. In examining the possibility of federation in colonial South Africa, he stressed the importance of mutual consent and of a deeper national conviction sustaining federal arrangements. Buchan ultimately recognised that durable federation cannot merely be imposed from above; it requires reconciliation of local identities with membership of a larger political union. Nigeria’s federal experience differs substantially from Buchan’s colonial setting, and some assumptions in his work belong to his race and era. But the general constitutional proposition remains relevant. A federation is not simply a map or an allocation of functions written into schedules and legislative lists. It is a continuous process of balancing unity with autonomy, national authority with constituent rights, and common purpose with legitimate diversity. In Nigeria, the Supreme Court occupies a central position within that balance. When the Federation and a state disagree over their powers, or states dispute rights between themselves, the Constitution provides an institution outside the immediate political contest to which such disagreements may be submitted. Section 232 is therefore not merely a technical provision on jurisdiction. It forms part of the architecture by which political disagreement is converted into legal argument and by which federal friction may be prevented from becoming political rupture. There is something profoundly civilising in this arrangement which Nigerian restructuring agitators seem to always overlook or remain unaware of. Instead of confronting one another through political pressure or public mobilisation, governments may appear as litigants and submit their claims to reasoned adjudication. Sovereignty under constitutional government is demonstrated not only through state power, but also through institutional dialogue, established procedures and acceptance of final lawful authority. The Supreme Court is an arbiter and national integrating institution. Its work helps to keep the disagreements of a diverse federation within a common constitutional language and culture. However, there is a paradox at the heart of judicial authority. Courts possess neither armies nor political constituencies. Judges do not campaign for votes, command the treasury or administer ministries, and remain largely invisible to the public. The strength of the judiciary rests upon something less tangible but enduring, which is public confidence in its independence, integrity and fidelity to law. This is why, in my humble opinion, judicial character matters. At the highest level, legal knowledge is indispensable but insufficient. A Supreme Court Justice must possess intellectual depth, patience, courage, independence of mind and awareness of institutional consequences. A judgment may settle one dispute while also establishing principles upon which many future controversies will be decided. A phrase written today can become part of the constitutional vocabulary of tomorrow. Judicial temperament therefore becomes an element of constitutional security. The qualities I observed in His Royal Highness, the Emir of Lafia, Justice Sidi Dauda Bage Muhammad I — composure, measured deliberation, dignity and the ability to listen before concluding — are attributes essential to an institution expected to pronounce finally upon matters already surrounded by passion. A judge in such a position must possess the discipline to resist not only political pressure but also public excitement and the intrusion of personal idiosyncrasies into decisions. Courts cannot determine constitutional meaning through opinion polls, nor can judges measure the correctness of their decisions by applause from one political tendency or denunciation from another. Courts are not beyond criticism, however. Their decisions must remain open to rigorous analysis by lawyers, scholars, the media, enlightened citizens and by history. Reasoned criticism forms part of constitutional democracy and can strengthen judicial authority. What must be protected is the distinction between criticism of judicial reasoning and destruction of confidence in adjudication. If every politically significant judgment is immediately interpreted as evidence of partisan allegiance merely because it disadvantages one side, the possibility of neutral constitutional authority becomes endangered. Sadly, this tendency has increasingly entered public consciousness in Nigeria. That is where a boundary must be established in the criticism of the Constitution and the Judiciary, as is often demonstrated by the misguided enthusiasm and exuberance of the proponents of restructuring in Nigeria. We concede that the Court must recognise that public confidence cannot simply be demanded. It must be earned through consistency, transparent reasoning, fidelity to precedent where appropriate and clear explanation where departure becomes necessary. Finality is a formidable power, and the obligation to explain must therefore be correspondingly greater. But that recognition is central to the selection and appointment of judges of the Apex Court. Judicial independence has institutional and ethical dimensions. Judges must be protected from intimidation and improper interference while remaining detached from partisan, sectional, confessional and personal considerations. This independence is not a personal privilege. It protects citizens and the state itself. Political fortunes are temporary, but constitutional institutions must aspire to permanence. The national interest must therefore be distinguished from the interests of any government, party, religion, region or influential personality. Against the fact that governments change, presidents leave office, legislatures get reconstituted and parties rise and fall, the deeper national interest lies in preserving the framework within which such changes can occur peacefully without imperilling the Republic. The permanence of the Judiciary is therefore the solid pillar upon which the Federation rests. This brings us to a distinction that should remain constantly in view. The Supreme Court must be profoundly conscious of the national interest, but it must never become a court of national expediency. By this I mean a situation where the Court arrives at a decision that may appear convenient at a particular moment. However, the overriding national interest is concerned with what principles will preserve constitutional government over time. The long-term stability of Nigeria depends not upon whether one side is accommodated today, but upon whether all sides believe that the same constitutional rules will remain available to them tomorrow and in perpetuity. This is why fidelity to law is itself a form of statecraft and the foundation of the national interest. The Supreme Court does not govern Nigeria, but it helps determine the constitutional conditions under which Nigeria can continue to be governed peacefully. Likewise, it does not manufacture national unity, but provides a mechanism through which disputes threatening that unity may be resolved under law. Although it is not a forum for discourse on governance, its judgments necessarily form part of public-policy development. In that sense, the Court is one of the custodians of the Republic. Its ultimate duty is neither to please government nor opposition, neither to satisfy popular sentiment nor to resist it for its own sake. Its duty is to uphold the Constitution with courage, wisdom, independence and restraint. Justice, in this larger sense, is not separate from the national interest. It is one of its highest expressions. These are the principles that I have learned in listening to The Honourable Justice Sidi Dauda Bage Muhammad I. The post The Supreme Court and national interest: The judiciary as a public-policy institution (2), by Usman Sarki appeared first on Vanguard News .
